articles.title: Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
articles.body:
Ousted general warned of years-long missile defense shortage before Iran war
Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.
George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.
He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month.
U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base.
CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels.
The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.
The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks.
The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.
"Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge."
An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years.
CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026.
The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs.
Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production.
In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year.
While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages.
One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels.
Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops."
He added that the U.S. still has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing."
"Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests."
How munitions are used around the world
The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge.
Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world.
The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long.
The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons.
But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address.
For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China.
There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen.
What led to the current weapons systems shortage?
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian.
"After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories."
He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did."
The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis.
Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting.
Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production.
"We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict."
Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries.
Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War.
Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory.

articles.title: Iran-US tensions soar as ships sink in Hormuz, fighting in Taiz
articles.body:
We're closing this live page now.
For more updates, head over to our new live page where we're continuing to track developments in the region.
This page is now closed. We're continuing to track developments on our new live page here.
These were the key updates earlier today:
•    Two ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz, one hit by a projectile and the other by a sea mine, as ongoing attacks impact maritime traffic.
•    Iran says it is preparing for war, but is also seeking diplomacy as reports suggest the US is mulling using its largest munitions if it resumes attacks.
•    Major fighting continues across multiple fronts in Yemen's Taiz, with significant casualties reported on all sides.
•    The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down a missile near Medina. The Houthis denied  launching the attack.
•    Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, West Bank, and south Lebanon despite any alleged agreements or supposed ceasefires.
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Yemen's Houthis on Thursday fired missiles at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the headquarters of the internationally recognised government, security sources told AFP, while a journalist saw smoke rising from the site.
"Houthi missiles targeted the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden," the government's interim capital, three local police sources said on condition of anonymity, after residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that he had previously spoken with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, in his first acknowledgment of direct contact.
Speaking at an election rally with Israel's Druze community, Netanyahu made reference to a bloody attack suffered by the Druze in Syria in July 2025.
"I called al-Sharaa. It was a very short, very sharp conversation, and the slaughter stopped," Netanyahu said, according to footage aired by Israel's public broadcaster KAN.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said on Thursday that regional actors had helped the Iran-backed group acquire "advanced technologies", without identifying those involved.
"The terrorist Houthi militias have worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki told a briefing in Riyadh, adding that the group now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
A Saudi foreign ministry official on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis in their ongoing fight with the kingdom, adding that Tehran continues to arm and train the group.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions," Dr. Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, said during a virtual briefing with reporters.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, said Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, have killed at least 17 people and injured 333 people between 7 and 11 October.
The 10 October attack on the airport was carried out with 10 drones, missiles and other projectiles, al-Maliki noted on Thursday.
A German court on Thursday jailed two men for apparently planning attacks on prominent pro-Israel public figures and spying on Jews on behalf of Iranian secret services.
The Hamburg court sentenced a Danish national, partially identified as Ali Hassan S., to eight-and-a-half years in prison for plotting deadly attacks.
His targets included the head of the German-Israeli society, Volker Beck, and the head of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster.
An Afghan accomplice, Tawab M., was sentenced to four-and-a-half years. Prosecutors said he had agreed to recruit a third man and provide him with a weapon for the attack on Beck.
The crimes were "terrorist activities orchestrated by Iran", judge Petra Wende-Spors said, adding the Danish national was preparing a contract killing "for purely political reasons".
Iran's army said on Thursday that a "violating" oil tanker is on fire in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement carried by state media.
"This rogue tanker, having disabled its tracking systems, was attempting to pass through the restricted area in the Gulf of Oman", the army statement added.
China's foreign minister voiced support for Palestinians on Thursday, saying China will continue to speak up for the Palestinian cause, according to a ministry statement.
"The Palestinian issue should not be marginalised," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Palestinian counterpart Varsen Aghabekian Shahin in Baku, the statement showed.
Wang urged "all peace-loving countries" to support the two-state solution, according to the statement.
Three years into the Gaza genocide, Britain’s pro-Palestine movement looks very different from when it first filled the streets in 2023.
When Israel first launched its attacks on Gaza, over a million people swarmed the capital.
Demonstrations took place weekly. But as the genocide continued unabated – killing tens of thousands of Palestinians, including thousands of children – protesters started to ask themselves: “What can I do?” Feeling that marching along police-approved routes was no longer enough. 
Read more below:
The United States is considering using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iran as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military strikes, raising questions about its devastating impact and whether it could penetrate Tehran's heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
According to a CNN report on Thursday, US military planners have drawn up options involving the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the "mother of all bombs" or MOAB, to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
Read more below:
Turkey’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that a mutual defense pact between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, as well as any deployment of Turkish forces under the agreement, requires parliamentary approval.
In a statement, the ministry also indicated that no final decision had been made on the type of assistance Turkey might provide to Saudi Arabia.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, and Turkish officials say it is expected to be ratified by parliament in the coming days. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and other officials have ruled out the deployment of combat troops, stressing that the pact is purely defensive.
A Hezbollah MP acknowledged Thursday that a 500-kilogram shipment of explosives seized last week by Lebanese authorities belonged to the group, a rare admission by the Iran-backed militants.
"The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" against Israel, lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said.
He said Hezbollah also called for the immediate release of those arrested over the seizure.
Fadlallah demanded the return of the shipment, seized on a road linking eastern Lebanon to Beirut, saying it constituted "capabilities" used by Hezbollah against Israel.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has said the state will no longer tolerate any possession of "illegal weapons".
Since a ceasefire in June, Hezbollah has not claimed any further attacks against Israel.
The EU and Gulf states have agreed to postpone their summit that was due to be held in Saudi Arabia on October 24, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday.
The sources confirmed remarks by Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who earlier on Thursday said he had understood the meeting would be scrapped due to security concerns.
Yahya Saree, the military spokesperson for Yemen's Houthis, claimed no attacks were carried out on Saudi Arabia today.
The announcement was shared after Saudi-backed coalition forces claimed a cruise missile headed towards Medina was intercepted and destroyed.
Yemen's Houthis say they have allowed the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to enter the besieged city of Taiz to assess the humanitarian situation amid ongoing heavy clashes.
Houthi official Abdulqader al-Murtada said the ICRC had made a similar request to Saudi-backed government forces in the city but had yet to receive a response.
He said this "should make it clear to everyone who is actually besieging Taiz".
Separately, the Houthi-run Saba news agency reported allegations that pro-government forces had released and armed 1,200 prisoners in Taiz and were using civilians as human shields.
Israel is blocking the construction of a military base in the Gaza Strip intended to house international troops under US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, delaying a key component of plans to stabilise and rebuild the Palestinian territory following Israel's genocidal war, according to a report by The Guardian.
The British newspaper reported on Wednesday that Israeli authorities had refused to allow contractors and construction vehicles into Gaza, more than two months after the US-led body awarded its first construction contract for the territory.
Read more below:
UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix on Wednesday urged the UN Security Council to begin negotiations on the future of peacekeepers deployed in Lebanon, as Beirut campaigns for an extension to the mandate set to expire at the end of this year.
A UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 but the Security Council last year ordered the mission to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence has issued alerts for potential threats in Najran and Jazan, state tv is reporting.
Millions could be thrown into poverty by surging energy costs, the impact of an intense El Nino phenomenon and higher interest rates, with vulnerable countries being pushed to the brink by repeated crises, the UN's development chief told AFP.
Global fuel prices have soared since the United States launched its war on Iran in late February, with Tehran's retaliations against Washington's Gulf allies curtailing major oil and natural gas supplies.
Fiscal deficits and debt-to-GDP ratios around the world have ballooned since the 2008 global financial crisis, with governments firefighting against a series of shocks including the pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, UN Development Programme (UNDP) head Alexander de Croo said many developing countries had responded to the current spike in energy prices with blanket subsidies, but a succession of crises had left them with limited resources to keep that up.
"You have to repair your roof while at the same time your home is on fire," he told AFP, adding governments in the developing world did not have time to rebuild buffers or resolve previous shocks before being hit by new crises.
The Global Alliance for Palestine hails unprecedented global solidarity, urging governments to turn support for Palestinians into action against Israel.
Read more below:
The International Monetary Fund expects energy-rich Middle Eastern economies to bounce back, but not in the medium term, the organisation's regional chief said on Thursday, as fighting continued between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis.
The statement comes as the IMF projects a widespread contraction in Gulf economies following months of war that began in Iran and has now spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen, with maritime energy traffic still impacted.
"We will not go back to the pre-war trajectory in the medium term because this shock will have a scarring impact on various sectors and also will disrupt a certain number of infrastructure, and will require additional spending in order to increase resilience," IMF regional director Jihad Azour told reporters.
Palestinian officials said Israeli strikes killed four people in Gaza on Wednesday, days after the anniversary of the declaration of an alleged US-mediated ceasefire.
Two young men died when Israeli forces struck a vehicle near Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip, civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal and Nasser Hospital said.
Two other people, including a woman, were killed when an Israeli aircraft struck an apartment building in Gaza City, according to Bassal and Al-Shifa hospital.
Since the alleged ceasefire, Israel has killed over 1,400 Palestinians.
The US military has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US officials familiar with the matter.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

articles.title: North Korea fires two types of submarine-launched missiles
articles.body:
- North Korea said it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Oct. 14, without Kim Jong Un attending.
- South Korean experts believe the missiles came from Hero Kim Kun Ok, marking the submarine’s first public missile launch since 2023.
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the Korean Peninsula on Oct. 14, state media said, in what South Korean analysts believe was the first missile launch from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, the submarine Pyongyang unveiled three years ago as its first “tactical nuclear attack submarine.”
The Korean Central News Agency reported on Oct. 15 that the country’s Missile Administration carried out the launches. It did not give flight times, distances or missile names, but released photographs of a submarine and of missiles climbing away on trails of flame. Based on those images, South Korean experts concluded the launch platform was the 3,000-ton-class Hero Kim Kun Ok.
“The test-fire aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems and contributed to getting the Navy skilled in performing its strategic missions,” KCNA said.
Kim Jong Un did not attend. Senior Workers’ Party official Kim Jong Sik and Missile Administration chief Jang Chang Ha oversaw the launches together with navy underwater weapons engineers, KCNA said, adding that the test had no adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launches on Wednesday but said the next day that it had tracked the missiles from before launch through the end of their flights, using assets it declined to identify because of confidentiality arrangements with the United States. A JCS spokesperson said one missile was fired from a vertical launch tube and the other from a torpedo tube, Yonhap reported.
North Korea launched Hero Kim Kun Ok, hull number 841, on Sept. 6, 2023, with Kim Jong Un saying at the ceremony that arming the navy with nuclear weapons could not be delayed further. Despite its label, the boat is a diesel-electric submarine rebuilt from an old Soviet-designed Romeo-class hull; the “nuclear” designation refers to the nuclear-capable missiles it is meant to carry. Until this week, the submarine had not been publicly seen firing a weapon.
Some South Korean analysts told Korea JoongAng Daily that the two weapons may have been a longer-range Hwasal-2 and a shorter-range Pulhwasal-3-31, a missile with a reported range of up to 2,000 km (1,240 miles) that North Korea says can carry its Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead. At that range, the missile could reach all of South Korea and U.S. military bases in Japan. One analyst quoted by the newspaper said firing two missile types with different speeds and approach paths at staggered times would make them harder for air defenses to intercept.
Cruise missiles fly low, often around 100 meters (330 feet) above the surface, which makes them harder to spot on radar than ballistic missiles. Unlike ballistic missile launches, cruise missile tests are not banned under United Nations Security Council sanctions on North Korea.
The previous submarine-launched cruise missile test North Korea reported came in January 2024, when Pulhwasal-3-31 missiles were fired from the smaller 2,000-ton-class experimental submarine 8.24 Yongung with Kim Jong Un watching. Earlier this week, North Korea also fired tactical ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the same sea.

articles.title: Could Israeli technology aid Saudi Arabia's struggles to stop Houthi missile attacks? - analysis
articles.body:
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 8, 10, and 11 killed at least 16 people. The deadliest strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309 others. On October 13, another attack damaged an administrative building at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. Saudi forces have intercepted numerous incoming weapons, but others have reached their targets despite the billions of dollars the kingdom has spent on air defenses.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Why are missiles and drones still getting through, and could Israeli technology help Saudi Arabia stop them?
Israel has spent decades developing defenses against different types of aerial threats. Some have already been supplied to the United Arab Emirates. In May, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help defend the UAE against Iranian attacks.
There have also been reports of Saudi-Israeli discussions about sharing intelligence through American military channels. Neither government has confirmed such an arrangement, but it raises the possibility of cooperation that would have been politically difficult to imagine only a few years ago.
Why are Saudi defenses struggling?
Saudi Arabia operates American-made Patriot missile batteries and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), which is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude. The kingdom’s first THAAD battery became operational in July 2025, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
These systems provide substantial protection, but the Houthis have weapons designed to exploit different weaknesses.
Ballistic missiles climb high into the atmosphere before descending at high speed toward their targets. Cruise missiles fly more like pilotless aircraft, sometimes close enough to the ground to escape radar detection until late in their flight. Drones can be smaller, slower, and much less expensive than the missiles used to shoot them down.
A defender facing multiple weapon types at once must identify each threat, choose the right interceptor, and respond before the weapons reach their targets.
A 2020 study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, The Missile War in Yemen, documented the Houthis’ growing arsenal of missiles and drones, developed with Iranian assistance, and their repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
The Houthis have since improved their capabilities. Regional officials told the Associated Press that investigators believe drones were launched ahead of cruise and ballistic missiles during the recent attack on Riyadh’s airport. If confirmed, the sequence would suggest an attempt to stretch Saudi defenses by presenting several threats in quick succession.
The kingdom has faced similar problems before.
After the September 2019 attacks on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities, Washington Institute for Near East Policy researchers Michael Knights and Conor Hiney examined gaps in Saudi radar coverage and weaknesses in the coordination of its defenses.
The weapons appeared to approach from the north, while much of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture was oriented toward threats from the east. Low-flying missiles and drones could take advantage of radar blind spots created by terrain, the curvature of the Earth, and the limitations of individual sensors.
The researchers recommended better coordination among existing radars, command systems, and interceptors, rather than relying solely on additional missile batteries.
Saudi Arabia’s geography presents another problem. The kingdom covers nearly 2.15 million square kilometers, approximately 78 times the combined land area of Israel and the West Bank. Its cities, airports, refineries, oil fields, military bases, and ports are scattered across enormous distances.
Israel’s much smaller geographic area lets some defensive systems cover several population centers or installations. Saudi Arabia needs far more widely distributed equipment, even though large stretches of sparsely populated desert do not require the same protection as major cities or oil facilities.
Cost is another concern. An inexpensive drone can force defenders to fire an interceptor worth hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.
Dr. Sidharth Kaushal of Britain’s Royal United Services Institute discussed the depletion of Gulf interceptor stocks and the difficulty of replacing them quickly in an April 2026 BBC interview. The Financial Times reported this week that Saudi Arabia was struggling with interceptor shortages and ongoing gaps in radar coverage.
Interception does not always prevent casualties. On October 13, debris from intercepted cruise missiles injured four people and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to Saudi Civil Defense.
Which Israeli systems could help?
Israel’s air defenses rely on several systems that operate at different ranges and altitudes. Iron Dome is the best known, but other Israeli weapons may be better suited to some of the threats Saudi Arabia faces.
Iron Dome was developed to intercept short-range rockets. Its radar tracks incoming projectiles and calculates where they are likely to land, allowing the system to focus on threats to populated areas or key installations.
Upgrades have expanded its ability to engage drones and cruise missiles. Iron Dome batteries could protect individual Saudi sites, but their coverage is too limited to defend much of the kingdom’s territory.
David’s Sling, developed jointly by Israel and the United States, is designed to intercept cruise missiles, certain ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones. Tests conducted in February 2026 included improvements intended to address newer aerial threats.
Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 are intended mainly for ballistic missiles. Arrow 3 can intercept suitable targets outside the atmosphere, before they descend toward the ground. Israel has used Arrow-family defenses against missiles launched from Iran and Yemen.
Such systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ballistic-missile defenses, but they would not solve the problem of detecting and intercepting a small drone approaching an airport at low altitude.
Two less familiar Israeli products could be especially useful for defending individual installations.
Rafael’s mobile SPYDER system is designed to engage aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles. Israel Aerospace Industries manufactures Barak MX, which uses different interceptors against aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and some ballistic threats.
Either could potentially complement Saudi Arabia’s existing defenses around oil facilities, airports, or military bases, provided the equipment could be integrated into the kingdom’s command and radar networks.
Iron Beam offers a different approach. Instead of firing an interceptor missile, it uses a powerful laser to destroy certain short-range threats. Israel delivered its first operational system to the military in December 2025.
The attraction is partly financial: Firing a laser can cost far less than using a missile against a relatively inexpensive drone.
Its limitations are substantial, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Lasers need a clear line of sight, and dust, haze, clouds, and distance can reduce their effectiveness. They cannot replace longer-range defenses against ballistic missiles.
Israel also operates C-Dome, a naval adaptation of Iron Dome that could help protect ships and offshore installations.
Which systems would be most useful to Saudi Arabia would depend on the targets it wanted to protect, the weapons it expected to face, and the equipment it already possessed.
How has Israel helped defend the UAE?
The United Arab Emirates offers the clearest example of Israeli air defense technology being used by an Arab country.
After Houthi attacks on Abu Dhabi in early 2022, Israeli defense sources told Breaking Defense that an agreement to supply Rafael’s SPYDER system was nearing completion. The publication subsequently reported that an Israeli-made Barak air defense system had been deployed in the UAE, although the precise model was not identified.
The two countries had established diplomatic relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords, removing a major obstacle to military purchases.
Their cooperation reportedly expanded during the 2026 war involving Iran.
On May 12, Huckabee publicly confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help operate them in the Emirates, according to the defense publication Janes.
The Financial Times reported that Israel had supplied additional equipment, including a version of Iron Beam, surveillance technology, and real-time intelligence about Iranian missile launches.
Those details have not all been independently confirmed. An October study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies discussed the reported laser and surveillance deployments but did not independently verify that they took place. Janes also noted that Huckabee’s remarks did not confirm those specific transfers.
There is no public accounting of how many incoming weapons were intercepted by Israeli systems operating in the UAE.
Still, the deployment of Iron Dome batteries and personnel establishes that the Israeli-Emirati defense relationship has moved beyond ordinary equipment sales. That experience may offer lessons for Saudi Arabia, although Riyadh has not normalized relations with Israel.
Could Saudi Arabia obtain Israeli assistance without normalizing relations?
Intelligence sharing would probably be easier to arrange than a weapons sale.
Information about missile launches and flight paths could potentially be relayed through American military channels, giving Saudi crews more time to prepare an interception without requiring Israeli launchers or personnel on Saudi territory.
Regional arrangements already support this kind of cooperation. In January 2026, US Central Command announced the establishment of a multinational air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. It aims to improve information sharing, joint planning, and coordination among regional military partners.
Israeli media reports suggest that Saudi-Israeli intelligence cooperation may already be taking place.
In September, The Jerusalem Post reported, citing a regional diplomat, that the two countries had discussed intelligence assistance through US Central Command. Ynet and Israel Hayom also reported, citing diplomatic and security sources, that Israeli intelligence was reaching Saudi Arabia through American channels.
Neither government has publicly confirmed those accounts, and it is unclear what information, if any, is being shared.
The Media Line reported in September that senior military commanders from Israel, Saudi Arabia, and six other Middle Eastern countries had attended a US-organized security meeting in Germany. US Central Command confirmed the gathering, but it did not establish a formal military alliance.
Saudi political analyst Abdulaziz Alshaabani warned against assuming that such contacts would lead to open military cooperation.
“Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” Alshaabani told The Media Line.
Purchasing Israeli missile defenses would raise additional problems.
Israel would have to authorize the export, and Saudi Arabia would need arrangements for training, maintenance, software, spare parts, and replacement interceptors. Some Israeli systems would also require American approval because of US involvement in their development.
Germany’s purchase of Arrow 3, for example, required Washington’s consent.
Political considerations could be harder to overcome than the technical requirements.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly insisted that diplomatic relations with Israel depend on the establishment of a Palestinian state. Its Foreign Ministry reiterated in February 2025 that it would not normalize relations without an independent Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.
A publicly acknowledged purchase of Israeli weapons would be considerably more difficult for Riyadh to explain than intelligence cooperation conducted through American military channels.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly announced an agreement to purchase Israeli missile defense systems, nor has it officially confirmed that negotiations for such a deal are underway.
Would Israeli technology solve the problem?
Israeli missile defense systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s defenses, but acquiring and deploying them would take time.
Saudi Arabia would need its own launchers, radars, trained crews, and interceptor supplies. Iron Dome batteries stationed in Israel are too far away to protect Riyadh. Any new equipment would also have to operate alongside the kingdom’s existing Patriot and THAAD systems.
Israel has its own shortages to consider after prolonged fighting with Iran and the Houthis. Its military needs to replenish interceptor stocks, which could limit the equipment available for export.
Saudi Arabia is also seeking assistance from established defense partners, including the US, Britain, France, Turkey, and Pakistan. Those relationships offer alternatives without the political complications of buying weapons from Israel.
Protecting civilians remains important even when interception fails. Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent attacks after September 29, leaving residents without official alerts before the deadly airport strikes. Warnings later resumed, including alerts issued by Saudi Civil Defense for Riyadh and Al-Kharj on October 14.
For Saudi Arabia, earlier warning of incoming attacks may be more immediately useful than new missile batteries. Better intelligence could help its existing defenses respond sooner, while new equipment would require procurement, deployment, and training.
A Saudi purchase of Israeli missile defenses would be a much bigger step, requiring decisions in Riyadh, Jerusalem, and possibly Washington. In the meantime, Saudi forces must defend widely separated cities and installations against missiles and drones that can approach from different directions, often with little warning.

articles.title: Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
articles.body:
Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Just two weeks ago, relations between Ukraine and South Korea seemed almost trouble-free. Russia and North Korea were deepening their military cooperation, North Korean soldiers were fighting against Ukraine, and Kyiv and Seoul appeared to have an increasing number of shared security interests.
On 23 September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in New York. They discussed strengthening political dialogue, trade, investment, Ukraine's reconstruction, and the common threats posed by military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
The meeting was a continuation of an eventful year in bilateral relations. In July, Volodymyr Zelenskyy met South Korean President Lee Jae-myung for the first time. Seoul announced an additional US$100 million in non-military assistance to Ukraine. Economic cooperation also held considerable potential: a framework agreement between the two countries provided for up to US$2.1 billion in preferential South Korean loans for Ukraine's reconstruction by 2029.
But on that very same day, 23 September, relations between the two countries began to deteriorate rapidly.
During his address to the UN General Assembly, Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Both soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025.
On the face of it, this should have been seen as an example of successful cooperation between Kyiv and Seoul. After all, South Korea had previously advocated the transfer of prisoners to its territory, where they could live in safety.
Instead, on 24 September, President Lee Jae-myung publicly accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. According to Seoul, the transfer was supposed to remain undisclosed to protect the prisoners themselves and their families still living in North Korea. Ukraine denied that any such agreement existed.
South Korea demanded an official explanation and an apology. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the situation as a diplomatic misunderstanding. His South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyun, later confirmed that he had received a letter of apology but said it fell short of Seoul's expectations.
On 2 October, Lee Jae-myung threatened Ukraine with further measures unless Kyiv acknowledged its breach of the agreement and issued a public apology. He also criticised Ukrainian statements about the threat of a military conflict between North and South Korea, accusing Kyiv of using rhetoric that could push the Korean Peninsula towards war.
On 8 October, the diplomatic crisis escalated to the recall of an ambassador: South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced its decision to bring its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, back to Seoul.
Ukrainian–South Korean relations had thus entered one of their most serious political crises since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
All this is happening as President Lee Jae-myung seeks to ease tensions with North Korea and restore inter-Korean dialogue. Pyongyang, however, has shown little interest in reciprocating.
Quite the opposite. On 7 October, Kim Jong Un sent Vladimir Putin a birthday message in which he called the Russian president his "dearest friend", reaffirmed his commitment to developing the strategic alliance with Moscow, and once again expressed support for Russia's "sacred war".
While Seoul is looking for ways to reconcile with Pyongyang, North Korean troops are gaining combat experience in Russia's war against Ukraine, and Moscow is helping North Korea develop its military technologies.
Why did the transfer of two prisoners of war provoke such a strong reaction from South Korea? Does Seoul's policy of reconciliation with Pyongyang stand any chance of success? What is North Korea gaining from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, and how could this change the balance of power on the Korean Peninsula?
Ukrainska Pravda spoke about these issues with Sangmin Shim, Senior Research Fellow at the Center for Foreign Policy and National Security at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, who specialises in international law and security affairs. His analytical articles and commentary on security and environmental issues in East Asia have appeared in international publications, including the American magazine The National Interest, as well as leading South Korean newspapers such as Chosun Ilbo and JoongAng Ilbo.
Although Shim is critical of certain policies and approaches pursued by the current South Korean administration, he is not a political opposition figure. His perspective is primarily that of an independent policy expert, shaped by his background in international law, diplomacy and national security. He previously taught international law at the Korea National Diplomatic Academy and has advised the government on legal and foreign policy issues.
The crisis in Ukrainian-South Korean relations
Ukrainian-South Korean relations are experiencing their first political crisis since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. South Korea recently even recalled its ambassador from Ukraine. Why has the issue of the two North Korean prisoners become so sensitive for President Lee Jae-Myung's administration?
Well, this is my personal take, but I believe the South Korean government is so pro-Russian that anything potentially sensitive for bilateral relations between North Korea and the Russian Federation is largely discounted. That is what we are seeing today. Even though Ukraine has graciously sent those North Korean prisoners to South Korea, the South Korean government is not really appreciative of it. South Korea is so preoccupied with normalising relations with the Russian Federation that the many gestures the Ukrainian government approaches us with do not really count from the South Korean perspective. This is a truly sad matter, in my view.
Did the situation with those two North Korean prisoners create any domestic debate in South Korea?
In the general public's view, it is great that these prisoners have been transferred to South Korean territory to live in a free state. But the current South Korean government is extremely worried about the consequences of having these North Korean prisoners on its territory.
They fear the possible negative effects of holding them in South Korean custody, which makes them highly sensitive about their presence. This is completely irrational from my perspective. South Korea has always strongly argued for the transfer of Korean prisoners of war to its territory, as the government deems these POWs to be its own citizens.
There is a total inconsistency in logic between the South Korean government's general policy and what they are doing in this specific situation.
Inter-Korean tensions
What we see in the news now is that the South Korean president wants to ease tensions and restore inter-Korean relations and dialogue. But how realistic is this when there appears to be very little interest in dialogue from North Korea?
This might be my personal judgement, but looking at the South Korean government's attempts to ease tensions with North Korea, I don't think it is going to happen. The North Korean government is completely focused on differentiating the two regimes. Pyongyang believes that any ties it might have with South Korea will not bring any real benefit to the prosperity of the North Korean regime. Therefore, the North Korean regime has decided to totally sever ties with South Korea, and that is exactly what they are doing. Unfortunately, the South Korean government is not ready to give up its hope for reconciliation with North Korea. This is where the real tragedy begins.
We also see that North Korea has physically reinforced the separation. They are building barriers, laying mines, and fortifying the border with South Korea. From your point of view, is this just another period of rising tension, or has Kim's "two hostile states" policy changed these relations?
From what I can see, North Korea is highly focused on differentiating between the South Korean and North Korean regimes. They started by laying mines to prevent South Korean troops from crossing into North Korean territory. This is extremely unfortunate, and as you know, it has led to unnecessary casualties among South Korean soldiers. I do not know how this issue can be resolved between the governments of South Korea and North Korea, but I really hope it will be smoothed over. I hope we can find common ground to talk to each other, with the understanding that this issue should not destroy us. There are still many factors that can influence a hopeful outcome in the future.
President Lee's opponents accuse him of being overly cautious about provoking North Korea. How strong is this criticism inside South Korea, and does it explain the unusually sharp reaction to Ukraine?
There is a deep political divide between the progressive and conservative fronts. The conservative front argues that any engagement with North Korea is basically a concession. Meanwhile, the progressive front believes it is a necessary step toward reconciliation. So, there is a huge divide regarding how they want to move forward in the current situation.
President Lee also criticised Ukraine's statement regarding a possible future conflict between North and South Korea, saying such rhetoric could push the peninsula towards war. Why is this topic particularly sensitive for him?
This is anyone's guess, but as I perceive it, a high-ranking official from the Ukrainian Presidential Office stated that ignoring the ties between North Korea and the rest of the world would have a ripple effect on South Korea's security. But is South Korea ready to accept that?
They believe that through peaceful inter-Korean relations, we will have better relations with every country south of the Korean peninsula. But this is unproven. So we will continue to have contentious relations with both the Ukrainian and North Korean governments.
The role of the North Korean military in the war in Ukraine
North Korea has already sent roughly 15,000 troops to Russia, and thousands of them have reportedly been killed or wounded. Before this, North Korea lacked military experience in such a large-scale war. How different is the North Korean army today because of its experience in Ukraine?
After sending their forces to defend or take over the Kursk region, those North Korean troops have gained valuable battlefield experience in modern warfare — particularly combining drone warfare with conventional warfare. From a South Korean perspective, this is not something we can easily discount. South Korea now needs to prepare for potential provocations from North Korea. However, the current government is not taking this seriously. Because this administration leans pro-Russia, pro-China, and pro-North Korea, they do not see these signs of provocation as something to truly worry about. I am sorry to criticise my government, but this appears to be the reality.
And have you already seen evidence that the lessons learned by North Korean soldiers have been incorporated into North Korean training or doctrine at home?
What I can see from the collaboration between North Korean and Russian forces is that the Russians have been sharing technical advice to further develop North Korea's military expertise — particularly in military tactics and drone warfare. Because of this, North Korean forces are in a better position. I do not know how else to put it, but those North Korean forces are now superior to South Korean forces in terms of dealing with drone warfare and other non-conventional forces involvement.
So, could you say that soldiers returning from Russia will eventually form a new, combat-experienced elite within the North Korean military?
First of all, the initial group sent to Russian territory consisted of combat troops from their special operations forces. They sent about 10,000 of their best elite troops, and the results speak for themselves. The involvement of these forces has genuinely contributed to retaking territories crucial to the Russians from Ukrainian control. This has had a major effect. I do not know if this trend can continue, because the North Korean government will also face difficulties with the continuous mobilisation of its armed forces. We do not know how the next stage will play out.
Let us look at the evidence the North Korean government is presenting. They are doing everything they can not to reveal the presence of their personnel on the battlefield. They want to limit their manpower to factories and other workforces – helping Russian forces and industries build stronger weapon systems. So, from what I perceive, North Korean personnel are not going to be seen anywhere near the front lines. But what I really want to emphasise in this case is that North Korea is collaborating with the Russian government and military to build up Russian stockpiles, ensuring the Russian military is prepared for incoming attacks from Ukraine or other countries.
We have a fairly good picture of what is moving from North Korea to Russia: soldiers, ammunition, and missiles. But we know much less about what is moving in the opposite direction and so from your point of view, what's North Korea actually getting in return from Russia?
I mean, what North Korea really hopes to gain from the collaboration with the Russian regime is that they will get military expertise in terms of ballistic missiles development and other top-notch military development. And in turn those current regimes will provide war forces in the form of manual labour and everything to provide the help necessary for the Russian Federation to rebuild their drone systems. So, then they will be able to compete with Ukraine in terms of non-conventional forces engagement.
The Russian government is seeing that the Ukrainian government will not be able to provide all the necessary supplies for all the necessary equipment for forever. And then this is going to be a kind of a war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine in which both will be subject to having to pay the highest consequences from this military conflict. This is so sad but this is also a fact.
If North Korea is developing the capacity to mass produce Shahed-type drones with Russian assistance, how would that change the threat facing South Korea and is South Korea prepared for the kind of mass drone warfare we have seen in Ukraine?
I mean, we have heard the most recent report from the National Security Advisor of the Korean Republic that if North Korea has been engaging too much in this Russia-Ukraine conflict, this would be the best opportunity for Korea to start taking over the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and making the whole Korean Peninsula as a unified nation. But this is not going to be the case that I have been seeing because this is not going to involve the political discussions between the major powers and basically the military aspect will not resolve the matters as we see it.
So what I perceive to be the case is that whatever happens in the territories between Ukraine and Russia will not have any consequences for the inter-Korean relations.
Inter-Korean relations will have to be dealt with by their own dynamics. Meaning that Russia, the United States, Japan, Korea and both North and South Korea will have to be sitting at the same table to negotiate away the differences. This is not going to be a short-term matter but it has to include the case of negotiations.
How Ukraine іs perceived in North Korea
Maybe you know how North Korean propaganda explains Ukraine to its own population? What have North Koreans been told about why their soldiers are fighting and dying thousands of kilometres from home?
I mean the North Korean government is ready to just decorate their lost lives as their national heroes. But this is not going to be the case if the loss of the lives and casualties continues to accrue for the North Korean regime. We have a report that records those current casualties at around 3,000 soldiers who have lost their lives and then another 33,000 soldiers who have basically lost their capability to re-engage in the world.
But with the intensification of the war and tensions within Russia and Ukraine, this will lead to more casualties for North Koreans. And I don't know if the North Korean government will be able to continue to persuade their general public with this loss of life as an unavoidable matter.
I don't know, but the North Korean government is not a democratic nation but they will not be subject to national approval or to answering the questions of the people but they will still feel the pressure from the North Korean populace about the loss of life that has been the consequence of the involvement of North Korean troops in the Ukrainian military conflict.
Is Ukraine portrayed as an enemy in its own right or is it simply as part of a larger confrontation with the United States and the West?
This is a really interesting question. Between the US and Ukraine, they don't seem to have much differences. But by just looking at the recent episode between the Ukraine and Republic of Korea, they seem to have some impending conditions to be dealt with between these two nations.
But from my perspective, these would be only diplomatic matters and if these matters were to be entrusted with both countries' foreign ministers, these differences will be easily negotiated away. What matters to Korea for now is that the current president of the administration. He's so active in voicing criticism about the Ukrainian government. This is not going to be helpful for settling the battle between Ukraine and South Korea. I really hope that the South Korean president will stay silent for at least for the next two weeks for the two ministers to be able to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement.
And from your point of view, how much do the average North Koreans actually know about the scale of their country's involvement in Russia's war?
From the conservative people's point of view, this government is so pro-North Korea and they suspect that North Korea has a huge influence over the matters of the South Korean government, but I don't believe this. But whatever is the case with the North Korean and the South Korean government, I suspect that the South Korean government needs to be in a better position to fight away the incoming threats from North Korea.
Basically in terms of cybersecurity and maritime security. But without those concerns, we have to see that the South Korean government is going to live their lives as if nothing has happened. This is not going to be a very positive case for the South Korean population.
And what happened with thousands of soldiers who return home with direct experience of Russia, of modern warfare, of modern technologies which are most likely not represented in North Korea?
I mean, these North Korean soldiers who have been sent back to the North Korean territories have returned with better experience with drone warfare and better experience with modern warfare. So they may have something to say to their military leadership. But what are considered to be the barricades with these North Koreans, they have been so exhausted with the too-stressful battlefield conditions. So, they may be the key. I mean, this is my hopeful suggestion, but these people will be the driving forces for asking for more changes regarding the South Korea and North Korea territories. And then, if the current administration fails to address these questions then there will be more political decisions, moving forward.
And could these people potentially be a problem for the regime now?
This is another matter that we don't really know the answer to. Military and civilian society have been in co-existence for a long time. But what I perceive in that case is that the military, they are taking the upper hand with the civilian structures. So whatever situation may arrive, it's going to be down to the hands of the military that will take the final decisions.
How South Korea іs helping Russia and what the consequences could be
What we see in the recent investigation by Reuters is that South Korean petroleum product experts have reportedly helped Russia with fuel shortages caused partly by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. How is this issue perceived in South Korea or is it even discussed there?
There are two different opinions about this matter. For conservative people, this is a really serious matter because it seems to be the case that the South Korean government is basically just looking away in the case of helping the Russian economy by support with petrochemical fuels.
But at the same time, from a purely technical perspective, the South Korean government is not prohibited from providing petrochemical products to the Russian Federation because this is not going to be subject to any country's sanctions regimes. So this is kind of revealing a kind of difference between many different countries' sanctions regimes.
From my perspective, it should be right to tighten the grip upon the differences in the different countries' sanction regimes. But at the same time, we have to hold our countries to settle out the differences between many unlike-minded nations to achieve the core missions of these sanctions which is to weaken the fighting ability of the Russian Federation in terms of the battlefield between the Russian Federation and Ukraine.
From the Ukrainian perspective this trade could be the next major source of tension between Seoul and Kyiv. From your perspective, how could these South Korean-Ukrainian relations be mended?
I mean, we have current issues between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea, but I strongly believe that this case will be settled away between the diplomatic negotiations between these countries.
What I perceive to be the more worrisome outcome is if the South Korean president Lee Jae-myung continues to press hard on the relations between Ukraine and the Korean Republic. And if that would be the case, then there's not going to be a case for these two bilateral regimes to be reconciled pretty much soon. Because as long as the president's mandate is not going to be met, there's not much that the South Korean foreign minister will do proactively to settle the differences. So all it might come down to is the president changing his position between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea.
In a way, the revealing of the identity of the prisoners, those North Korean soldiers, would not be so much to disrupt the bilateral relations between these countries. It's really important that the South Korean government is so aware of this importance and also about the importance of not being too far away from these two government's positions.

articles.title: Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
articles.body:
Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
Reduced missile warnings increase threat to civilians as Trump pushes an ‘energy ceasefire’ and peace negotiations.
Kyiv, Ukraine – The supernova-like blasts of exploding Russian ballistic missiles are followed by thunderous thumps, shockwaves, fires and deaths – and the staccato of Ukrainian air defence systems.
This week’s nightly attacks on Ukraine that killed at least 15 and wounded dozens resembled hundreds of previous raids – with one exception.
The air raid sirens began howling just seconds before or after yet another wave of missiles struck apartment buildings, power plants and warehouses.
But Ukraine’s partners did not provide the country with intelligence data from NATO’s early-warning satellites, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as tensions between Washington and Kyiv rise.
He did not name the United States and President Donald Trump has denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence.
The constellation of military satellites detects Russian ballistic missile attacks by the rockets’ thermal flames seconds after launch.
The warnings give Ukrainians up to 10 minutes – precious, life-saving time to sound air raid sirens and send emergency text messages to prompt evacuations to bomb shelters.
“That’s what helps prevent the killings,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s ground radars can only detect the incoming missiles as their speed ranges from 6,000 to 12,000km/h (3,730 – 7,260 miles per hour).
‘Trump pressures our president’
Despite Trump’s denial, Ukrainian observers have a simple yet harrowing explanation – the US president wants to help Republicans win more congressional seats in upcoming midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv into declaring an “energy ceasefire” with Moscow that would drive global oil prices down.
“Trump pressures our president, pressures Ukraine” as he strives to “get advantage by any means necessary in the election campaign,” Lieutenant-General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s general staff of armed forces, told Al Jazeera.
The lack of intelligence data “significantly affects the effectiveness of air defence, we don’t have time to respond,” he said.
Without the satellite data, Ukrainian drones and missiles also “lose precision when striking targets deep in Russia,” he said.
On Sunday, Trump announced the ceasefire that envisages no mutual strikes on energy infrastructure – from Russian oil refineries and fuel depots to Ukrainian power and heating stations.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media.
Kyiv said the announcement was a surprise, while Moscow declined to say whether it backs the idea – and kept on hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The pressure goes beyond the refineries as Trump wants to quickly reopen, arbitrate and complete peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow – even if they benefit the Kremlin.
“He needs peace talks to succeed. Ideally, it is a certain unblocking of the peace settlement process, when Kyiv shows more willingness to agree with Russia’s demands,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
The pressure will continue until “Kyiv shows readiness for a compromise and concessions towards Russia,” he said.
Moscow “simply abuses” the pressure and the suspension of air raid warnings to escalate attacks on Ukraine, he said.
Kyiv’s ‘priority’: The destruction of oil refineries
The suspension of data-sharing was especially shocking, given that Kyiv did stop hitting Russian refineries for three days.
It was only on Wednesday that its drones attacked refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions, said Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksander Novak.
However, Kyiv’s focus on striking oil refineries is ineffective and counterproductive, another observer said.
“Kyiv’s strategic priority is still the destruction of oil refineries,” Nikolay Mitrokhin of Germany’s Bremen University, who has penned hundreds of authoritative analyses of the hostilities, told Al Jazeera.
However, Russia overcame the initial shock by transporting gas from refineries in Siberia and exporting it from neighbouring Belarus and Kazakhstan.
No economic collapse, massive joblessness or public protests followed the strikes, while Moscow continued its air raids, adding jet-powered drones that resemble cruise missiles and are hard to down with Ukraine’s existing air defence system, he said.
“What is the basis for Kyiv’s and its backers’ conviction that strikes on oil refineries and depots will lead to Russia’s strategic defeat before Ukraine is defeated? I don’t understand,” he said.
However, Ukrainian attacks on data centres, bridges and factories where drones are assembled are far more effective, he said.
Recent strikes on data centres of Russian online giant Yandex and the state-run Sberbank resulted in disruptions of services in Russia and even former Soviet republics where Yandex operates its online payment, food delivery and taxi services.
Trump “didn’t ask him to stop the war, to give away cities or stop striking Russian rears in general,” Mitrokhin said.
Kyiv has repeatedly reiterated that it was ready to start peace talks if they are preceded by a ceasefire, but Moscow wanted to continue ground assaults and air raids until the peace terms were finalised – which could take months or even years.
‘We’re ready for any turn of events’
On Wednesday, Ukraine’s drone czar accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite terminals that are part of the military-grade Starshield system.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said that SpaceX abruptly and without any warning limited services for terminals placed on drones flying over 160km/h (100mph).
The limit affected crucially-important interceptor drones and followed Trump’s request, presidential adviser Serhii Sternenko said.
Musk said that the White House owns and controls the Starshield systems and that any limits on speed are decided by Trump.
Some military analysts warn that the limit may be followed by a total shutdown of Starlink for Ukraine that could damage the quality of all military communications.
“But we were getting ready for everything,” Andriy Pronin told Al Jazeera. “We already know it may happen, that’s why we’re ready for any turn of events.”
In September 2022, Musk secretly ordered engineers to switch off Starlink coverage in the Russia-occupied Kherson region, effectively thwarting Kyiv’s push to retake it, Reuters reported.
In 2023, Musk threatened to cut off Ukrainian military access to Starlink unless the US defence department took over the costs.
Later, the Pentagon, Poland and other European allies took over the costs.

articles.title: A month of strikes could leave three of Ukraine’s megacities without electricity, water, and heat: NYT reveals Russia’s plans
articles.body:
A month of strikes could leave three of Ukraine’s megacities without electricity, water, and heat: NYT reveals Russia’s plans
Kyiv • UNN
According to the NYT, Russia could launch 70 missiles, 720 drones, and 150 aerial bombs at Ukraine over the course of a month. Three cities are reportedly being identified as targets.
Russia plans to launch approximately 70 ballistic missiles, 720 long-range drones and 150 guided aerial bombs at Ukraine within 30 calendar days, in order to cause the collapse of electricity, heating and water supply systems in Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing an article by The New York Times.
Details
The enemy's main targets could be Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa.
The publication's journalists analyzed data from Ukraine's Air Force and concluded that the indicated number of ballistic missiles and drones approximately corresponds to the average monthly number of such weapons that penetrate Ukrainian air defenses. Therefore, the NYT is convinced that Russia may attempt to inflict critical damage on Ukraine's energy system within one month—damage it failed to achieve during the previous four winters.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa are under the greatest threat
If Russia's scenario is implemented, the three largest cities identified as the main targets could face a large-scale disruption of municipal infrastructure. According to the enemy's plan, analyzed by the publication's editorial team, Russia seeks to reduce electricity supplies to Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa by 90%, and heating supplies by up to 90%. Missile and drone attacks could also cause serious disruptions to water supplies and sewerage systems.
Such a development would trigger a large-scale humanitarian crisis, especially in conditions of low temperatures, when the stable operation of power grids, boiler houses and pumping stations is critically important for ensuring the functioning of cities.
Why Russia's plan to black out three Ukrainian megacities could become reality
According to the publication, Ukrainian officials and analysts fear that Russia currently has significantly greater capabilities to carry out a large-scale air campaign against Ukraine's energy sector than in the previous years of the full-scale invasion. The reasons cited include the depletion of Ukrainian air defenses, a reduction in American military aid, and Russia's expansion of missile and drone production.
In addition, after several years of systematic Russian shelling, Ukraine's energy infrastructure remains vulnerable. Because of accumulated damage, even one successful strike may have consequences that previously required the enemy to carry out several attacks to achieve.
The shortage of interceptor missiles for American Patriot surface-to-air missile systems also "plays into the hands" of the Russian Armed Forces. These systems are among the most effective means of protection against Russian ballistic missiles, which pose a particular danger to critical infrastructure facilities.
In addition, the situation is complicated by the continuous improvement of Russian weaponry. Over the years of the war, Moscow has increased the number of missiles and drones in its arsenal and improved the effectiveness of their use. And Ukraine's "mirror" strikes on Russian energy facilities, including oil refineries, cannot inflict damage on Russia's economy on the same scale as the damage Russian attacks cause to Ukrainian infrastructure, officials and experts interviewed by the publication note.
What is known about Russia's plan to destroy the energy system
Earlier, The New York Times reported on a document that the Ukrainian side presented to European partners as an intercepted Russian plan for a large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system. According to the journalists, the plan envisages phased strikes on energy facilities, including electrical substations and hydroelectric power plants, with the aim of disrupting the operation of the entire energy system.
A separate threat is the possible disconnection from the power grid of three Ukrainian nuclear power plants that remain under Ukraine's control.
But it should be noted that the NYT editorial team emphasized that it was unable to independently verify the authenticity of the document. It is also currently unknown whether Russia will implement the described scenario and how successful such a campaign could prove to be.
We remind you
On October 14, Russian forces launched another massive attack on Ukraine, damaging dozens of energy facilities in Kyiv and Kharkiv. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity. Russian strikes also affected railway infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine bins 'energy cease-fire' with attacks on Russian refineries
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared the end of a brief, unreciprocated truce amid growing rift with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks.
The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the cease-fire, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Ukraine never stopped its strikes on Russian refineries. It wasn't possible to independently verify each side's claims.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for Ukrainian defenses and attack operations.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We’re done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4 1/2 years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy cease-fire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
