articles.title: Houthis launch deadly attack on Yemen presidential palace
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen's Aden
The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government's interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.
The attack hit command centres located inside the presidential compound used by government forces and the Saudi-led military coalition that supports them, a Yemeni minister said on condition of anonymity.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government it backs have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.
Government military sources in Yemen said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in Thursday's strikes on Aden's Al-Maashiq palace in the divided country's south.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani had been present at the time, but "was not harmed in any way".
The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces with three missiles, and another for Saudi-led coalition forces at the complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.
Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them".
Yemen's civil war - in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 - reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.
Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.
Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," said Dr. Rayed Krimly.
The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.
Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired "several ballistic missiles" at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
Oman meeting refused
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.
Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times this month.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
He added the group had "worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors", saying they now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
(AFP)

articles.title: The Gulf needs a security order that Washington cannot switch off
articles.body:
The Gulf has spent decades buying security from the world’s most powerful military. American bases dot the region, advanced weapons fill its arsenals, and defence agreements bind its rulers to Washington. Yet the war involving Iran has exposed a troubling paradox. The Gulf’s security arrangements may help deter adversaries, but they cannot guarantee that the region will escape a conflict shaped by decisions made elsewhere.
The consequences are no longer confined to military installations or oil terminals. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz threatens energy exports and maritime commerce, while attacks on critical infrastructure jeopardise the economic transformation programmes on which Gulf governments have staked their futures. Wealth can finance reconstruction, but it cannot restore lost confidence overnight.
The problem is not that the United States has become irrelevant. Its intelligence, airpower, naval capabilities and logistical reach remain difficult to replace. Nor does greater independence mean that Iran’s regional ambitions should be ignored. Rather, the Gulf faces a structural dilemma: the states most exposed to escalation do not necessarily possess the greatest influence over the decisions that produce it.
That dilemma demands a different ambition.
The Gulf does not need a security order without Washington. It needs one that can survive Washington’s changing priorities. The objective should be to turn external protection into one pillar of regional security, rather than the foundation on which everything else depends.
The limits of an American security umbrella
For decades, American military power has underwritten the security of the Gulf monarchies. The US Fifth Fleet operates from Bahrain, while Qatar hosts Al Udeid Air Base, a major centre for American air operations. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have invested heavily in American aircraft, missile defence and other advanced systems. These arrangements provide capabilities that would be costly and difficult to reproduce independently.
But military protection is not the same as strategic control. Washington ultimately decides how to deploy its forces, which threats deserve priority and when military action serves American interests. Gulf governments can influence these calculations through diplomacy and cooperation, but they cannot assume that their preferences will prevail.
The distinction becomes critical when Washington’s objectives collide with the region’s exposure to retaliation. An American operation may be designed to weaken an adversary or restore deterrence, yet its consequences can fall disproportionately on neighbouring states whose ports, airports, energy facilities and shipping routes become vulnerable. The presence of American forces can strengthen deterrence without eliminating the risks associated with escalation.
Recent events have also exposed the limits of military expenditure as a measure of security.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Saudi Arabia spent an estimated $83.2 billion on its military in 2025, making it the Middle East’s largest military spender. Nevertheless, sophisticated arsenals cannot automatically prevent attacks by adversaries using drones, missiles and other asymmetric capabilities.
The lesson is not that American protection has failed or that Gulf governments should abandon their alliances. It is that a security model built around external military superiority leaves too much dependent on decisions that regional governments cannot control. A durable system must preserve the benefits of American power while reducing the consequences of its possible absence, inconsistency or strategic redirection.
READ: Gaza’s future is not Washington’s to decide, says rights chief
Why the Gulf cannot secure itself alone
Reducing dependence on Washington, however, is easier said than done. The Gulf Cooperation Council has existed since 1981, yet its members have struggled to translate shared vulnerabilities into a fully integrated security system. They differ in their perceptions of Iran, their relationships with outside powers and their preferred responses to regional crises. Their rulers also remain reluctant to surrender sovereign authority over national defence.
These divisions matter more than the number of weapons purchased. A regional security order requires compatible warning systems, reliable intelligence-sharing, coordinated responses and clear procedures for consultation when a crisis erupts. Without these mechanisms, neighbouring states may possess formidable individual capabilities while remaining collectively vulnerable.
Nor would replacing American dependence with a collection of new foreign partnerships solve the problem. Saudi Arabia’s expanding defence relationship with Pakistan and Turkey illustrates the search for additional strategic options.
Their Mecca Joint Defence Agreement promises closer military cooperation, including coordination among their armed forces. Such arrangements can broaden the Gulf’s choices, but their value will ultimately depend on operational coordination, credible commitments and the ability to respond effectively under pressure.
The danger is that diversification becomes an exercise in accumulating partners rather than building regional capacity. Multiple alliances can offer useful insurance, but they can also create competing expectations and overlapping commitments. A state that depends on several external powers without developing its own mechanisms for crisis management may remain exposed to the same underlying problem.
Iran must also be part of the equation. No credible Gulf security order can simply assume away Tehran’s military capabilities, its regional relationships or its ability to threaten maritime commerce. Yet treating Iran exclusively as a target to be deterred leaves little room for managing incidents before they become wars. Deterrence and diplomacy are not alternatives; each is more effective when the other exists.
The challenge, therefore, is political as much as military. Gulf governments must recognise that national security cannot be secured through bilateral relationships alone when threats cross borders and the consequences of conflict spread across the entire region.
Building an order Washington cannot switch off
A more resilient security order should begin with practical cooperation rather than grand declarations. The GCC needs stronger mechanisms for sharing intelligence, coordinating early warning and integrating air and missile defence. Common operating procedures would help governments identify threats, distinguish deliberate attacks from accidents and coordinate responses before confusion escalates into confrontation.
Second, the region needs institutionalised crisis diplomacy. Direct communication channels, maritime incident protocols and regular consultations involving Gulf states and Iran could reduce the danger of miscalculation. Such arrangements would not resolve every dispute or eliminate the need for deterrence. Their purpose would be narrower but essential: to prevent individual incidents from triggering a regional conflict that no government can easily contain.
Third, economic resilience must become part of security planning. The International Monetary Fund has highlighted the potential benefits of completing the GCC Railway and Saudi Landbridge projects, which could reduce economic losses during a closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative energy routes, diversified shipping arrangements and stronger regional logistics would likewise give governments more options when maritime traffic is disrupted. Infrastructure should be assessed not only by its commercial return, but also by the strategic flexibility it provides.
Finally, Gulf governments must define more clearly what collective security means in practice. Which threats require immediate consultation? How should members coordinate assistance after an attack? What commitments can each state credibly make, and how can those commitments be implemented without undermining national sovereignty? Answering these questions will be more valuable than announcing another ambitious pact whose operational foundations remain uncertain.
None of this requires the United States to withdraw. Washington can remain an indispensable partner, providing capabilities that regional states cannot quickly replicate. But a stronger regional framework would also make that partnership more sustainable by giving Gulf governments greater agency, reducing the risk of unilateral escalation and ensuring that essential security functions do not depend entirely on decisions made abroad.
The ultimate test of Gulf power is not how much its governments spend on weapons or how many foreign partners they can attract. It is whether they can shape the conditions under which their people, economies and infrastructure remain secure.
The Gulf cannot dictate Washington’s choices, any more than it can eliminate rivalry with Iran. It can, however, build institutions, capabilities and diplomatic channels that make those choices less decisive for its future. That is the difference between being protected by a powerful ally and possessing a security order of its own.

articles.title: Who Are the Houthis and Why Are They Attacking Saudi Arabia’s Airports?
articles.body:
The European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council on Thursday announced the postponement of a joint summit set to take place in Saudi Arabia next week, amid safety concerns prompted by Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom.
Citing the “continued attempts by the terrorist Houthi militia to target the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its civilian infrastructure, which threatens the security and safety of innocent civilians,” the council said the Gulf-European Summit will be rescheduled.
The postponement comes after Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Wednesday vowed to forge ahead with the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities, just hours after striking oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters.
“Operations toward Saudi depths will continue in the coming days,” said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, describing the locations as “legitimate targets” and framing their attacks as a direct response to Saudi strikes on Yemen. Saudi-led forces said they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday and local journalists reported hearing “loud blasts” in the Saudi capital.
The escalation follows weeks of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The conflict reignited amid the widespread fallout of the U.S.-Iran war, bringing further instability to the Gulf region. In September, the Houthis said they had captured the strategic Perim Island that sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime chokepoint. They also seized other islands in a bid to tighten their grip on the Red Sea coastline. Amid fears that a stronger Houthi position along the coast could further constrain global energy supplies, Saudi-backed forces recaptured key areas around the strait in early October. The Houthis have since ramped up their focus on Saudi Arabia’s airports and energy infrastructure.
Tuesday night’s attack on Aramco’s executive offices in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a limited fire, Saudi’s Ministry of Energy confirmed. No injuries were reported. TIME has reached out to Aramco and the Saudi government’s media office for further information. Saudi authorities said several missiles and drones had been intercepted elsewhere, and that falling debris injured four people in the capital of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia launched strikes on an oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital Sanaa on Tuesday, as the tit-for-tat attacks escalated.
The Saudi strike on the oil depot appeared to be in response to the Houthis’ attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left over 300 injured. A projectile hit that same airport on Sunday, killing one person, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed. The week before, an attack on Abha International Airport killed two people and wounded 28, said GACA.
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. However, it is struggling to defend itself against the Houthis, who are positioned to strike deep into the kingdom. The Saudis are currently investigating how their defense systems failed to stop the deadly attacks. Experts cite the vast mass of Saudi land as one reason why defensive measures may have failed. The Saudi border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles. “Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” said Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, in an online post.
Operations at King Khalid remain suspended in the wake of the attacks. Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Philippine Airlines are among the carriers to announce a suspension of flights to Riyadh.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans in the country of “potential flight cancelations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” stipulating that U.S. government employees now require “special authorization” to use any airport in the country.
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the Houthis “are behaving very badly.” In a Truth Social post, he continued, “I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the hell out of them and, at their request, stopped,” seemingly referencing the U.S. strikes between March and May last year, which came in response to the Houthis attacking vessels in the Red Sea and disrupting global trade. Weeks after the strikes began, a cease-fire between the U.S. and the Houthis was reached via Omani mediations.
On Saturday, Trump suggested that the U.S. may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. Asked about the possibility of U.S. strikes, a senior U.S. official told TIME that Washington is “in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability and we will always fulfill our commitments to our partners.”
As tensions in the region continue to escalate, here’s what to know about the Houthis, their history with Saudi Arabia, and why they are attacking airports.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis are a political and armed group in Yemen that first emerged in the 1990s and have been fighting the country’s internationally recognized government for around two decades. The group is a revivalist movement for Zaidism, a branch of Shi‘ite Islam. The Zaidi muslim population in the country represents around 35% of the Yemeni population.
The Houthi movement was largely born from a transformation of the Believing Youth Forum (BYF), according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The group became known as the Houthis in honor of their founder and leader, Hussein al-Houthi. Before he was killed by Yemeni forces in 2004, al-Houthi had developed the group into a more militarized movement. The group is now led by his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi.
Civil war broke out in 2014 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, forcing the government to flee to the southern city of Aden. Since then, the group has been engaged in fighting against a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government. The Houthis currently have control of most of the country’s west, including Sanaa.
Experts compare the Houthis to authoritarian regimes on account of the social restrictions imposed in areas under the group’s control and alleged human rights abuses.
“The Houthis are dominated with very ideological and radical ideas, like a Zaidi ISIS. They have similarities also with the Taliban in terms of social control," says Mahmoud Shehrah, a Yemeni political analyst at London-based think tank Chatham House.
How are the Houthi rebels linked to Iran?
The Houthis hold strong ties to Iran, often taking action in line with Tehran’s objectives.
“Since 2009, Iran [has] started to speed up weapons supplies, training, but also a lot of funding to the Houthis,” says Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemeni research fellow at Chatham House, noting that links between the two began as early as the 1990s.
The Houthis are often considered part of Iran’s proxy network, known as the “Axis of Resistance,” which also includes Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Islamic Resistance network in Iraq, and previously the Assad regime in Syria, until its collapse in December 2024.
In response to the Israel-Hamas war, the Yemeni militia launched several strikes on shipping vessels in the Red Sea, disrupting global trade in late 2023 and the early months of 2024. The U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024 for a series of strikes on Houthi targets across Yemen in retaliation for the attacks on unarmed vessels. The U.S. carried out an additional campaign against Houthi targets later that year.
The Houthis entered the Iran war in March by firing a barrage of ballistic missiles at southern Israel. In the months since, the group’s advances along the Red Sea are widely considered to serve the interests of Iran. A Houthi blockade in the region against Saudi Arabia was declared in July, and several vessels have been attacked. The threat that the Houthis could bring another critical maritime chokepoint to a standstill, much like Iran has done with the Strait of Hormuz, could give Tehran significant leverage in its negotiations with Washington.
However, experts say it’s not entirely accurate to call the Houthis a direct proxy.
"The Houthis are one of the more independent regional allies of Iran in the Middle East. They have their own independent interests, even though their interests converge regionally and globally,” says Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.
Even so, the Houthis have become increasingly vital for Iran. “With the fall of Assad, with the weakening of Hezbollah, the Houthis became the most important regional ally Iran has,” says Al Muslimi, pointing specifically toward the Houthis' ability to disrupt trade in the Red Sea.
What do the Houthis want?
The group’s goals have changed over time, as regional developments have unfolded, experts note.
“The Houthi's ultimate goal is to be a regional power,” says Al-Muslimi. With regard to the reignited civil war, the Houthis ultimately want an end to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory.
“The Houthis want to have the skies and the ports of the country open for trade, for goods and services,” says Gerges. “They want money to flow into the coffers of the Houthis.”
The civil war has had a disastrous effect on Yemen, with nearly half of the population in government-controlled areas facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the United Nations. “The current situation is very dire for the Yemeni population, but also for the ability of the Houthis to rule Yemen effectively,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis want to consolidate rule and regime. They want to be recognized as the legitimate government in Sanaa, as opposed to being considered a non-state actor,” he adds.
When did the Houthis and Saudi Arabia begin fighting again?
A cease-fire brokered by the United Nations in April 2022 largely held for over four years, before collapsing in July. The Houthis claimed Saudi Arabia had launched strikes on Sanaa Airport, targeting a Houthi delegation returning from Iran. In a move they framed as retaliatory, the Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia.
“The Houthis saw this as a golden opportunity to change the balance of power against Saudi Arabia and Yemen itself and launch a lightning offensive,” says Gerges.
Following further strikes on Houthi targets later that month, the militia group began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, belonging to the state-owned petroleum company Aramco.
In September, strikes on oil refineries and other related facilities ramped up, and Saudi Arabia’s airports became a target.
Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports?
Prior to the 2022 cease-fire, attacks on airports were largely considered a signature move of the Houthis.
In a highly-publicized attack, the group struck Abha International Airport in June 2019, injuring at least 26 people, Saudi authorities said. The strike earned international condemnation and was deemed a possible war crime by Human Rights Watch.
Now, after fatal strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the Houthis have threatened to keep targeting airports. The main motivation behind these attacks is the economic and geopolitical pressure they apply to Saudi Arabia, experts say.
“The Houthis want to put severe pressure on the Saudi Arabia economy, airport infrastructure, and security,” says Shehrah. “They want to squeeze Saudi Arabia's arms to push them to a political settlement.”
The unrest threatens to have a strong economic and political impact on Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman's governance. The disruption is “costly” to him, says Al-Muslimi, who notes that Bin Salman is eager for Saudi Arabia to be seen as a “safe harbor.”
The financial and reputational damage of these strikes has also put the Saudi public on the frontline of the conflict. It’s a “shock, because it's the first time in years that such major attacks have targeted deep inside Saudi Arabia,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis are trying to exert tremendous pressure on the leaders of Saudi Arabia to force them to accept conditions for lifting the blockade on Yemen and recognizing their legitimacy,” he continues. “Although, I doubt that the Saudi leadership will concede to Houthi demands… this would be seen as a surrender and humiliation."

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Kyiv observed the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump, only to face intensified Russian attacks and slower Starlink satellite communications.
Source: Financial Times
Details: "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy said in a forthright interview with the FT in London. He also sharply criticised Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent affinity for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Asked to explain the relationship between the two leaders, Zelenskyy said Trump has an instinctive affinity for autocrats and extremely wealthy people.
"He [Trump] speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong," Zelenskyy said.
The FT noted that Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that a moratorium on the attacks, together with an agreement to purchase hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel, is necessary to bring down fuel prices in the US.
Zelenskyy said he had suspended strikes on energy facilities for three days to accommodate the US request. However, Moscow continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure and kill civilians, with more than 100 people killed in the past week.
The president also said that, despite Ukraine suspending its strikes, its forces had been left without US early-warning systems for incoming ballistic missiles. Starlink satellite communications, operated by Elon Musk's company, had also been slowed across the country, making battlefield operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military facilities more difficult.
The FT wrote that the deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington marks the most serious crisis between Ukraine and its most important security partner since the Oval Office spat in February 2025.

Asked whether Ukraine would stop striking oil refineries even if Russia continued its attacks, in an effort to repair relations with the White House, Zelenskyy said he would agree to do so only if the US supplied him with more American-made Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine says one Neptune strike wiped out six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers at Borisoglebsk, taking a chunk out of the fleet Russia uses to hammer the front with guided bombs.
Ukraine’s Navy says a Neptune missile strike on Russia’s Borisoglebsk military airfield destroyed six Su-34M fighter-bombers overnight on October 15, potentially dealing a major blow to one of the aircraft fleets Moscow relies on heavily for guided-bomb strikes against Ukrainian troops and frontline cities.
According to the Ukrainian Navy, the strike was carried out with a Neptune coastal missile system against the airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Six Su-34M aircraft were destroyed, along with ground equipment used to support flight operations, while secondary explosions and a fire were recorded across the base.
“On the night of October 15, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine struck the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region using the Neptune coastal missile system,” the Navy said.
“As a result of the strike, six Su-34M bombers were destroyed. Technical equipment supporting aviation operations was also destroyed, while secondary detonations and a fire were recorded on the airfield grounds. Information is being clarified.”
The Su-34M is a deeply modernized version of Russia’s Su-34 all-weather supersonic fighter-bomber and was developed as an evolution of the aircraft intended to replace the older Su-24M.
The modernization substantially expanded its avionics, reconnaissance capabilities, electronic warfare systems, and range of precision weapons.
The aircraft can carry multiple guided and conventional aerial bombs at the same time, along with various missile types. Russian forces have relied heavily on the Su-34 family to launch glide bombs fitted with UMPK guidance and wing kits, allowing aircraft to strike Ukrainian positions and settlements from well behind the front line.
The Su-34M modernization also introduced improved communications, navigation, weapons-control equipment, and reconnaissance pods designed for electro-optical, electronic, and radar intelligence missions. The aircraft’s two pilots sit side by side inside a heavily armored titanium cockpit.
Its expanded weapons suite includes precision-guided bombs, cruise missiles, and anti-ship weapons, while upgraded electronic warfare and radar systems are intended to improve survivability against air defenses.
Ukraine’s Navy said destroying the aircraft would reduce Russia’s ability to conduct tactical aviation missions in the affected sectors and weaken the fleet used for guided-bomb strikes against Ukrainian forces and communities near the front.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries after Zelensky condemns withdrawal of US intelligence
articles.body:
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian refineries with a strike at an installation in the Ryazan region, the regional governor said on Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced his anger at a "dangerous" withdrawal of US intelligence.
Since US President Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, Kyiv had refrained from attacking Russian refineries, which the US leader had blamed for raising diesel prices on global markets.
But Zelensky had voiced increasing frustration with Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, which he said on Wednesday had left 600,000 people without power. He warned that Ukraine would not suspend its own attacks indefinitely if Russia did not reciprocate and also criticized what he said was Trump's favoritism toward Russia.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, he said Ukraine's patience had run out.
"The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” he told the newspaper.
Pavel Malkov, the governor of Ryazan, said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the region had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
"The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene," he said.
In his interview, Zelensky criticized Washington’s eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump’s apparent admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump calls for Ukraine to replace Zelensky after announcing Russia diesel deal
Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky and railed against Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, one day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia, aiming to lower fuel prices that have soared since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
Despite Ukraine's suspension of refinery attacks, Ukrainian officials complained that they had not received any US early-warning alerts in recent days for incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
They also said the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications service had been slowed across the country, hampering frontline operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military sites.
Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X/Twitter that Starshield - the military version of Starlink - was owned and controlled by the US government, which decided on any limits on speed.
Zelensky has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In the FT interview, Zelensky said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he dismissed the idea that failures of the Starlink satellite system might have been caused by a fault.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT.
Zelensky demands US interceptors in exchange for halting strikes on refineries
Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, he told the newspaper he could only agree if, in return, he was given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable.
"We didn't destroy any relationship," he said, claiming it wasn't up to him to repair US-Ukraine relations.
Ukraine claims to have damaged six Russian military aircraft
Ukraine's military said on Thursday it had damaged six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region.
In a Telegram statement, Ukraine's military general staff said it had confirmed damage of varying degrees to all six aircraft.
The Su-34M is a large fighter-bomber, costing tens of millions of US dollars apiece and frequently used by Russia to drop devastating glide bombs onto Ukrainian cities near the frontline.
Ukraine said on Telegram that it used its Neptune coastal missile system in the attack.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Kremlin condemns Ukraine refinery strikes as ceasefire violation
The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts, after a Ukrainian drone struck a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia did not perceive that Ukraine had ever complied with an energy ceasefire announced last week by Trump. Ukraine says it paused such strikes for three days but resumed them after Russia continued to attack its own energy sector.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Ballistic missiles struck Kiev and the surrounding region on Tuesday and Wednesday night before air raid sirens could warn residents to take cover.

articles.title: Houthi attacks threaten to strain Pakistan-Iran relations: Analysts
articles.body:
Escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are testing Pakistan’s ability to defend a longstanding security partner without damaging relations with neighboring Iran, with experts warning that deeper military involvement could carry consequences at home and across its borders.
Islamabad’s dilemma brings together two relationships it has strong reasons to preserve – a defense and financial partnership with Riyadh, and cooperation with Tehran on border security, trade, energy and regional diplomacy.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on Aug. 7, treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all three. This month, the countries agreed to implement their collective defense commitments amid attacks on Saudi territory.
“Pakistan cannot stay idle as it has committed itself to Saudi Arabia's defense,” Umer Karim, a doctoral researcher at the University of Birmingham, told Anadolu.
But defending the kingdom against the Iran-backed Houthis could undermine Islamabad’s efforts to deepen ties with Tehran and facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States, he added.
Saudi Arabia’s importance to Pakistan extends beyond military cooperation. Riyadh has provided financial support to help Islamabad manage pressure on its external finances, including a pledge in April of an additional $3 billion finacial assistance alongside an extension of an existing $5 billion deposit.
Iran’s importance rests partly on geography. The countries share a 909-kilometer (565-mile) border, making cooperation over militancy, smuggling and cross-border movement a practical security concern.
Relations combine cooperation with recurring mistrust. In January 2024, the countries exchanged cross-border strikes against militant targets.
Both have nevertheless sought closer economic ties. In August, they agreed to expand trade, improve customs coordination, energy cooperation and activate joint border markets, pursuing a $10 billion annual trade target and a free trade agreement.
Christoph Bluth, professor of international relations and security at the University of Bradford, described Pakistan’s approach to Iran as pragmatic cooperation combined with strategic caution.
Tehran was an important neighbor, he said, but not a strategic ally on the same level as Saudi Arabia or China. The defense agreement could create friction without necessarily causing a breakdown in relations.
“The decisive question is implementation,” he told Anadolu. “If it develops into what is perceived as an operational anti-Iran or anti-Houthi coalition, it would seriously damage Islamabad-Tehran relations.”
Iranian lawmakers have criticized Pakistan’s growing military alignment with Saudi Arabia.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei expressed concern this month over reports of a possible large-scale Pakistani troop deployment, adding that he hoped it was only a "rumor."
Bluth described Tehran’s response as divided. Some lawmakers had warned of retaliation if Iran were attacked from pact members’ territory, while the Foreign Ministry had indicated it did not presently regard the agreement as directed against Iran.
Pakistan’s leaders have sought to offer reassurance. President Asif Ali Zardari said Tuesday that the pact was “purely defensive and not directed against any country.” Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi security the following day.
Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry has also said its forces would defend Saudi territory rather than cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis. On Friday, it said that Pakistan has deployed a “substantial” number of military forces and resources in Saudi Arabia.
Bluth considered participation in a ground war unlikely, with involvement instead potentially focused on air and missile defense, intelligence, training and protecting Saudi territory.
“Pakistan has agreed to provide rapidly deployable forces, but their numbers and precise mission remain undisclosed,” he said.
“A defensive role would cause tension with Iran but could remain manageable,” he added. “If it comes to direct operations against the Houthis, that would risk a major diplomatic crisis.”
Karim said Pakistan’s existing military presence in Saudi Arabia demonstrated its commitment to Riyadh.
“Pakistan's military is already on the ground within Saudi Arabia, which signifies Pakistan's resolve to stand by its Saudi ally,” he said. "It's only a matter of time that it will become whether directly or indirectly involved against Houthis," he said.
According to him, the Iranian side clearly does not view this positively and "is likely to express its disappointment mainly through unofficial channels and also by mobilizing pro-Iran constituencies within Pakistan."
Arhama Siddiqa, a research fellow at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad, emphasized the distinction between defensive cooperation and offensive operations.
“Pakistan has clarified that the agreement is defensive and does not envisage cross-border operations against the Houthis in Yemen,” she told Anadolu.
Instead, Islamabad has an interest in encouraging restraint and a negotiated settlement to prevent wider conflict and preserve constructive relations with Iran, she added.
The experts differed over how deteriorating relations with Tehran would affect Pakistan.
Karim argued that security conditions had already worsened on both sides, limiting the additional impact of a diplomatic downturn. He also expected relatively limited consequences for energy cooperation because economic links remained weak.
Bluth, however, warned that strained relations could weaken intelligence-sharing and border management, giving armed groups greater room to operate across the frontier between Pakistan’s Balochistan and Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan provinces.
“It could also aggravate sectarian tensions inside Pakistan,” he said.
Border commerce, local livelihoods and Iranian electricity supplies could suffer, alongside prospects for the Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline and wider energy cooperation.
The principal danger, Bluth said, was not conventional war but “a more unstable border, intensified insurgency and increased security risks for Pakistan.”
Siddiqa similarly warned that weaker cooperation could allow non-state actors to exploit vulnerabilities, while disrupting trade, border markets, connectivity and energy projects.
“The two neighbours face common challenges relating to cross-border terrorism, militancy, smuggling and border management, making sustained security coordination indispensable,” she said.
Neither country would benefit from further border instability, she added, stressing the importance of maintaining diplomatic and institutional contacts.
Pakistan’s role in brokering talks between Tehran and Washington, which led to the Islamabad Memorandum in June, gives it another reason to preserve relations with Iran.
Islamabad has served as an intermediary between the two sides, and Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said Iran reaffirmed its trust in Islamabad’s mediation during President Masoud Pezeshkian’s June visit.
But Karim said those diplomatic efforts were increasingly in conflict with the security demands arising from Houthi attacks and renewed fighting in Yemen.
Bluth argued that mediation did not require complete neutrality. Iran’s continued willingness to exchange messages through intermediaries, including Pakistan, suggested that trust had not entirely collapsed.
“Pakistan must keep its Saudi commitment restricted to defensive measures, maintain direct consultation with Tehran and support political engagement with the Houthis,” he said.
“If Pakistani forces participate in direct offensive operations against the Houthis or Iran, it is unlikely it can sustain its role as mediator,” he added.
Siddiqa said the defense cooperation did not inherently contradict Pakistan’s role as a facilitator. Effective mediation, however, depended on maintaining trust, credibility and open communication.
Karim was more pessimistic that Pakistan could act as a mediator while also engaging in the Yemen conflict.
“It will be extremely difficult, and eventually Pakistan will have to choose one side,” he said.

articles.title: Turkish army buys CAKIR ground-launched cruise missiles
articles.body:
- Türkiye signed a contract with Roketsan for land-based ÇAKIR cruise missile systems for the Turkish Land Forces, defense industry chief Haluk Görgün said.
- ÇAKIR is a jet-powered cruise missile with a range of more than 150 km and a 70 kg warhead.
Türkiye has signed a supply contract with missile maker Roketsan for land-based CAKIR cruise missile systems for the Turkish Land Forces, Haluk Görgün, head of the country’s Presidency of Defense Industries, announced on Oct. 15.
Görgün said in a post on X that the contract is meant to strengthen the army’s long-range strike capability, and that more than 200 subcontractors took part in the project, including nearly 20 large and medium-sized companies.
“We have signed the ÇAKIR Project Supply Contract for land-based systems to enhance the strategic strike capabilities of our Land Forces,” Görgün said, in a statement translated from Turkish.
Roketsan’s ÇAKIR is a compact, jet-powered subsonic cruise missile that can be fired from aircraft, armed drones, ships and uncrewed surface vessels, as well as tactical wheeled vehicles. According to the company’s specifications, the missile weighs up to 275 kg (606 pounds) on its own and up to 330 kg (728 pounds) with the solid-fuel booster used for ground and ship launches. It carries a 70 kg (154-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 150 km (93 miles).
The missile is powered by the KTJ-1750 turbojet engine developed by Turkish firm Kale R&D. Its guidance combines inertial navigation with jam-resistant satellite navigation and a radar altimeter, so it can keep flying on course under heavy electronic jamming. Roketsan says ÇAKIR can fly very low over water or follow terrain to stay below enemy radar, and that its airframe uses radar-absorbing materials. The family includes land-attack, anti-ship and electronic warfare versions with different seekers.
Roketsan carried out the first publicly announced ground launches of ÇAKIR in August, when two missiles fired from a mobile launcher hit separate land and sea targets, Naval News reported. Indonesia’s ambassador to Türkiye said the same month that his country had bought ÇAKIR missiles, and the missile has been linked to Qatari fast attack craft projects.
Görgün placed the deal alongside Türkiye’s other surface-to-surface missiles, saying deliveries of the BORA and TAYFUN ballistic missiles to the army are continuing while ÇAKIR and the land-based KARA ATMACA cruise missile add to the country’s deterrent. Roketsan made its first delivery of KARA ATMACA, a ground-launched version of the Atmaca anti-ship missile, to the Turkish Land Forces in April 2026.
He said Türkiye is expanding serial production of missile and air defense systems to meet demand from its own army and from friendly and allied countries, as part of a wider push to make the Turkish defense industry fully independent.
The contract brings a ground-launched cruise missile with a 150-km reach into Turkish army service alongside the longer-range KARA ATMACA and Roketsan’s ballistic missiles, with more than 200 Turkish subcontractors involved in its production.

articles.title: North Korea tests submarine-launched cruise missiles amid tensions with South
articles.body:
North Korea has test-fired two distinct types of cruise missiles from a submarine, its state media reported, following weeks of friction with South Korea triggered by a landmine explosion along their heavily fortified border.
The projectiles were launched on Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries", the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) confirmed.
The official news agency said the latest tests "aimed to examine the current mobilised posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a naval exercise, highlighting the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK".
Submarine-launched capabilities remain a critical objective for Pyongyang, offering lower-altitude flight profiles that complicate detection and radar interception compared to traditional ballistic weapons.
Tactical significance
State-media photographs showed one projectile emerging vertically from the sea, trailed by thick smoke, while a second missile breached the water's surface at a 45-degree angle.
Accompanying imagery depicted a projectile skimming horizontally over open water alongside a surfaced submarine.
The test forms part of a wider tit-for-tat escalation across October, with both nations testing hypersonic technology.
South Korea launched its first domestic hypersonic glide vehicle last week, days after Pyongyang announced tests of an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic weapon.
The two Koreas remain technically in a state of war after the 1950–1953 conflict concluded with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
Saudi Arabia on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis in the dramatic escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic republic continued to arm and train the group.
In a virtual briefing with reporters including AFP journalists, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude oil exporter, has come under sustained attack by the Houthis in recent days, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
It has launched retaliatory strikes on Houthi strongholds in Yemen - one of the world's poorest countries - but the Iran-backed group remains undeterred.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions," said Dr. Rayed Krimly, the deputy minister.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
The official said the kingdom continued "to have direct communications with Iran", but added: "Overall, it doesn't seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution."
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
"This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago."
Airport strikes
On Saturday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and wounding around 300 others, in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Thursday said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times in October.
During a presentation in Riyadh covering the strikes, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
"The terrorist Houthi militias have worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors," he said, adding that the group now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
Yemen's civil war reignited in July after a years-long UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The situation took a sharp turn for the worse in September, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them capture swathes of new territory in Yemen, including along the Red Sea coast where a waterway crucial to global energy flows is located.
On Thursday, the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the headquarters of the internationally recognised government, security sources told AFP, while a journalist saw smoke rising from the site.
"Houthi missiles targeted the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden," the government's interim capital, three local police sources said on condition of anonymity, after residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions.
Since their offensive began, the Houthis have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government whose forces they are battling on the ground.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
(AFP)

articles.title: F-35 Drops 8 Bombs in Quick Succession During ‘Ripple’ Test
articles.body:
The Marine Corps recently conducted its first-ever “ripple” release of eight Small Diameter Bomb IIs from an F-35B, a key early step in proving out the capability for all F-35 variants.
A “ripple release” refers to munitions all being released in one pass instead of multiple go-arounds. Marine aviators from the Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron 1 at Yuma Proving Ground, Ariz., conducted the test Sept. 15, retired Air Force Maj. Gen. Jon Norman, Raytheon’s vice president for air and space systems, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
SDB II, also called “StormBreaker,” is a 250-pound, low-yield, precision-guided munition that can hit moving targets in all weather conditions at ranges of at least 46 miles. It is a joint effort between the Air Force and Department of the Navy and is built by RTX’s Raytheon.
While software and other issues have delayed fielding StormBreaker on the F-35, the “ripple” capability could be critical to the Lockheed Martin-made stealthy fighter down the line, Norman argued.
“From a pilot perspective, it’s nice because you’re not sitting there exposing yourself when you have eight targets to address,” he said.
It also eliminates the need to do hands-on weaponeering for each bomb.
“You address the entire target set, so it’s less workload in the cockpit, and you’re able to achieve an effect that I think the pilots are really going to appreciate,” Norman said.
The networked missiles can also be confined to a defined kill box to ensure they strike only a specific area on the battlefield.
“We’re able to set boundaries,” Norman said. “So, you give it a kill box, and it’ll exclude everything outside of that and only hit within that kill box.”
That’s a key upgrade for the StormBreaker compared to what the bomb is replacing—cluster munitions. SDB II was developed to give pilots an option to replace legacy-era cluster munitions following the 2008 DOD policy directive, which set a 2019 deadline to stop using the area-saturation weapons that had high failure rates and could produce swaths of unexploded ordnance on battlefields.
So, a pilot could spot a boat swarm, quickly set the parameters, and then launch eight 250-pound missiles to destroy the mini-fleet in one pass, Norman said.
“Through automated target recognition software that’s built into it, we can hit prioritized threats,” Norman said. “So, if one fails or one gets shot down, then they just reorder the prioritization.”
F-35 Tests
Low-rate initial production on the StormBreaker started in 2015, and the Air Force cleared the bomb to go on its “objective” aircraft, the F-15E, in 2020. But the service hopes to integrate the munition onto many more platforms, including the F-35A. The Navy, meanwhile, cleared the SDB II to go on its F/A-18E/F this February, though its objective aircraft remains the F-35B and C.
But while the F-15 and F/A-18 carry the StormBreaker externally, the F-35 uses its internal weapons bays to maintain stealthiness, offering a new wrinkle to the ripple release process. The F-35B has the smallest internal capacity of the variants, to accommodate the fan that enables vertical landings.
The next ripple release test is planned for this quarter over a small range in Texas, Norman said.
“We’ll take those results then to the Air Force and to the Navy and the Marines and say, “we’ve demonstrated this capability, is this something you’re interested in?’” Norman told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Future tests could include striking moving targets at sea with multiple munitions, Norman said—a particularly relevant capability, given reports of swarming boat attacks by the Iranian military in the Strait of Hormuz.
As Raytheon works on refining the “ripple eight” capability for operational use, the F-35 fleet is awaiting rolling software patches to fully incorporate the StormBreaker into its arsenal.
A July report from the Government Accountability Office noted that “SDB II initial capability on the F-35 is delayed 2 years, and program officials said that it might be delayed 2 more years due to F-35 software development issues.”
The F-35 fleet has undergone its third technology refresh, or TR-3, which upgraded the L3Harris core processor, replaced the aircraft’s memory storage unit, and installed multicore processors. But while a “truncated” version of TR-3 was completed in 2025, the fleet is still getting software patches to continue upgrades.
“Development on TR-3 was completed in 2025,” Lockheed Martin spokesperson Mireya Villarreal told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “We continue to build on this baseline through the Block 4 modernization program, which implements upgrades including additional weapons, electronic warfare capabilities and improved sensor technology to ensure the warfighter can defeat any threat.”
StormBreaker’s Future
in addition to the ripple release test, Norman said Raytheon is working to extend the StormBreaker’s 46-mile range by exploring engine efficiencies and design work on the bomb’s body.
“We don’t want to constrain pilots,” Norman said. “We want to give them their full operating envelope to be able to release this.”
At the program’s inception, the Pentagon planned to acquire 21,160 StormBreakers, but that figure has now risen to 31,800, according to the GAO report
“Last year we produced and delivered 1,500 StormBreakers. This year we’re increasing that,” Norman said. He could not provide specific numbers for this year’s deliveries.
“But it’s a significant increase, and we have capacity in the factory to increase more,” he said.

articles.title: Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better

Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better

They all came. Help came from NATO… So, basing on that, I must say that NATO is working well and the US is a partner in NATO. Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following NATO and also Article 5."

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after a three-day halt due to an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy expressed support for his US counterpart's proposed energy ceasefire, but claimed Russian strikes continued despite Kyiv’s halt.
“That's it. Block is out,” Zelenskyy said, responding to a question about how much longer Ukraine will maintain a halt to energy strikes.
On reports that the US suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Zelenskyy said that over the course of Ukraine’s three-day halt to strikes in Russia, his country was subject to ballistic missile attacks and did not receive any early warning alerts.
He said Washington had earlier warned Kyiv about the blocking of intelligence if it did not stop strikes on Russian energy sites.
“This is, I think, the problem. And when it goes together with Starlink's decision, which is 100% the decision of American side … I think that (it is) not (about) military people. I think it's about SpaceX. So together it makes huge problems,” Zelenskyy added.
Zelenskyy said he told Trump that Ukraine will "destroy" Russia's ballistic missile launchers if Starlink opens on Russian territory.
He argued that if a diesel deal, such as the one announced over the weekend, forces Ukraine to be silent on the battlefield, then questions will arise concerning "when the next deal will be," which would "definitely" concern Russian gas.
The Ukraine leader said he does not want to interfere in "diesel deals," but Ukraine will respond to Russian strikes.
"The question (is): can you give me missiles for Patriot (systems), because when I will not attack them because you asked me not attack them, they will attack me. It's fair if you will give me with what to defend.
"It's the minimum what I ask. No? I think yes. And when I'm asking this, your answer is blocking Starlink," he added.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a freelance adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said on Wednesday that speed restrictions were implemented on Starlink satellites in Ukraine, limiting their speed to 100 mph (161 kph).
"Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," Beskrestnov added.
US billionaire Elon Musk said Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government," and decisions on speed or usage restrictions are made by the US military and ultimately the president.
Separately, Zelenskyy told British journalist Piers Morgan that he felt "betrayed" over the diesel agreement between Russia and the US.
He said he is "sure that they knew what they did," commenting on a question on whether the speed restrictions on Starlink satellites were implemented deliberately.

articles.title: South Korea tests vehicle-mounted laser against drones
articles.body:
- Hanwha Systems said its Cheongwang laser and a 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser destroyed all three target drones during a South Korean Army exercise.
- South Korea began fielding Cheongwang in December 2024, and Hanwha puts the cost of each laser shot at about $1.50.
South Korea’s Cheongwang laser air defense weapon and a 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser shot down all three target drones flown against them during a South Korean Army exercise on Oct. 14, manufacturer Hanwha Systems said.
The demonstration took place during the Army TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise hosted by Republic of Korea Army headquarters, in front of about 500 attendees including the army chief of staff, military officials, academics and industry representatives. Hanwha did not say how far away the drones were, what types were used, how long each engagement took, or how the three targets were divided between the two lasers.
Cheongwang, which means “light of the sky,” is the official name of the Laser Air Defense Weapon Block-I, developed by Hanwha Systems with South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development. Instead of firing missiles or shells, the system focuses a high-energy beam on a drone until its structure or electronics fail, and it keeps firing as long as it has electrical power. Hanwha puts the cost at about $1.50 per shot, in line with the roughly 2,000 won figure South Korea’s arms procurement agency has used since 2024.
South Korea began fielding Block-I in December 2024 and calls it the first operationally deployed laser weapon in the world. About five units have since been installed at major state facilities, including the Ministry of National Defense building in Seoul, and the system is rated in the 20-kilowatt class, Korea JoongAng Daily reported. The same report said engineers have since built a domestic laser oscillator, the core component that generates the beam, to replace a German-made part.
The program grew out of a December 2022 incident in which five North Korean drones crossed into South Korean airspace, one of them reaching the northern edge of Seoul, and fighter jets and attack helicopters failed to shoot any of them down. South Korea started developing the laser in 2019 with a budget of 87.1 billion won, and officials have kept its engagement range classified. The procurement agency has also acknowledged that Block-I struggles in rain and fog, a common limit for laser weapons, and plans a more powerful Block-II.
Hanwha said Cheongwang also destroyed four drones and two larger unmanned aircraft in a row on Sept. 16 at the 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition organized by South Korea’s defense ministry.
“Laser weapons are core assets that will fundamentally change the game of air defense,” said Joohun Shin, head of the Laser Systems Business Center at Hanwha Systems.
Hanwha is developing a 50-kilowatt laser armored vehicle with its own money, aimed at export customers, and displayed it at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, which opened Sept. 8. The company has not named any foreign buyer, and it did not provide specifications for the 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser used in the Oct. 14 demonstration or say whether the South Korean Army plans to buy it.

articles.title: Trump and Putin’s ‘terrible’ alliance threatens to strain EU’s resolve on Ukraine
articles.body:
Traditional matryoshka dolls depicting Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump pictured in a tourist shop in downtown Moscow on Oct. 21, 2025. | Olesya Kurpyayeva/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will make a direct pitch to European leaders for more help on Friday, amid a crisis of faith among allies over Donald Trump’s latest steps favoring Russia.
At the second day of an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy joins European prime ministers and presidents as they discuss Ukraine’s need for more weapons and cash, with concern growing that Kyiv faces a shortfall of billions of euros next year.
The reality of the threat to European security from the four-year-long war penetrated the summit bubble after air drones hit two ships in or near Romanian waters, prompting emergency talks with NATO.
Advertisement
“We all in Europe want this war to end,” Zelenskyy said on social media as he arrived in the Belgian capital on Thursday. “And for that, signals of strength are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine.”
It is especially important, Zelenskyy said, to “act together to protect lives.” But unity among European leaders is in short supply at a meeting already riddled with tensions.
EU governments are pitted against each other in their own fraught negotiations over how much money to commit to the 27-country bloc’s budget. With populists surging, discontent raging and elections scheduled in major power centers across the continent, under-pressure leaders are a long way from approaching a deal.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels on October 15, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
That’s the combustible mix of financial discussions the U.S. president waded into.
Trump’s decision to open up American markets to previously banned Russian diesel — intended to ease price pressures in the U.S. — risks tilting the balance of an expensive war in Russia’s favor, three European officials warned. Putin’s war chest can now swell from additional fossil fuel exports, while Ukraine struggles for cash.
As they arrived for the first day of the marathon two-day gathering on Thursday, EU national leaders began informally discussing options for how to help redress the balance. That discussion should to be picked up again around the summit table on Friday.
Advertisement
Russian assets
One idea rapidly rising back up the agenda is the fraught question of whether, or how, to make use of some hundreds of billions of euros of frozen Russian financial assets held in European banks.
The bulk of these rest with the Euroclear depository in Brussels. A previous attempt to grab the funds and send them directly to Kyiv was blocked by the Belgian government ― and other countries less prominently ― over concerns it would be exposed to legal action.
But Sweden, Finland and Germany want to take another look at the assets. The European Commission is to come up with a new detailed assessment of Ukraine’s funding needs and an options paper on how to help, including the use of assets, according to officials from these countries.
As the summit began, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had been urging his counterparts to “do everything we can to help Ukraine get through the winter and continue to support it next year as well.”
“We will also have to increase funding once again in order to provide Ukraine with truly long-term assistance,” he said. “I remain firmly convinced that we are not only defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity, but also the political order of Europe, which is truly under pressure from Russia in every respect.”
A German official earlier suggested that of the available options to help Ukraine, including a loan and direct grants from national governments, using the assets was the most viable way forward and should be “discussed.”
Advertisement
A U.S. proposal to unfreeze some of the Russian assets and transfer them to a U.S.-controlled entity so Washington could use them as leverage in peace talks with Moscow also attracted strong criticism.
Merz told reporters that the assets had been frozen in Europe and “should remain frozen in Europe … That is our business, and we will decide on it.”
‘Try again’
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo told POLITICO as the summit began: “The best solution would be that we will have a solution on how to use frozen assets … We have to try again.”
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo speaks to journalists at the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Sept. 14, 2026. | Jouni Porsanger/AFP via Getty Images
Sweden is also backing the move to re-examine options on using the assets to help Ukraine’s future funding needs. “Doing nothing is not an option,” Swedish EU Affairs Minister Jessica Rosencrantz told POLITICO. “The Commission is looking into different financial options, and we need to get them on the table quite soon,” she said.
Leaders at this week’s summit should “be really honest that Ukraine needs increased financing” and that the EU “must really step up,” she added.
Zelenskyy met Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, the main opponent to a deal on assets, for talks on Thursday and thanked him for his country’s support so far.
Speaking to reporters after the first day of the summit, De Wever said the assets should be looked at as part of a future peace agreement. “Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is: Yes there are,” he said. “Are they in this building? They are. Are there outside this building? Yes there are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don’t.”
Advertisement
For Finland’s Orpo, Trump’s “terrible deal” with Putin on diesel, and the apparent U.S.-imposed limits on Starlink technology to help Ukraine counter Russian attacks, are hard to understand.
“My message to [Trump] is that we are allies,” Orpo said in an interview. “We are in NATO. And what is the biggest threat against NATO? It’s Russia — and that is why there is no logic. I don’t have answers. I have many questions.” He said Trump may be focusing on winning votes ahead of next month’s midterm elections in the U.S. but he should remember that his real allies lie in Europe and he should not “trust” Putin.
Election anxiety
Finland holds its election next year at the same time as what could be a seismic contest in France. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls for the French presidency and wants to cut aid to Ukraine and slash the EU’s budget.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who is constitutionally barred from standing next year, warned EU leaders that they must get a deal on the bloc’s next budget by December, otherwise it will be too late.
But the 27 leaders remain split and show no signs of bridging the gap between “frugal” countries like Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands, who want to limit the settlement, and others such as Italy and Romania, who are on the side of bigger pots of cash for regional development and farming.
European Council President António Costa also sees the urgency. He believes a deal before the end of the year is not only necessary but achievable, according to two EU officials.
Advertisement
Costa, who is taking over the negotiations from Ireland in its role at the helm of the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, believes failing to secure a deal by December would push the entire budget negotiating process beyond the electoral cycle. That would potentially delay a deal until October next year — perilously close to the new EU budget taking effect in January 2028.
In an effort to make progress on the budget talks, EU leaders will return to Brussels for an extra summit next month.
Camille Gijs, Hanne Cokelaere and Gregorio Sorgi contributed reporting.

Bloomberg: UK provides Ukraine with additional long-range Storm Shadow missiles
