articles.title: ACC Mulls Commercial Counter-Drone Services for Air Base Defense
articles.body:
Air Combat Command is looking for defense firms capable of providing a private counter-drone service, complete with the personnel to operate it, for defending air bases across the Air Force.
ACC, which oversees the service’s Point Defense Task Force, is conducting a market survey to identify companies specializing in counter-small unmanned aerial systems defense technology that can provide “C-sUAS as a Service,” according to an Oct. 13 solicitation.
According to the solicitation, the intent of the service model is to:
- Provide organic, resilient, sustainable, and agile Point Defense capabilities across Department of the Air Force installations
- Implement a flexible, scalable architecture allowing installations to scale operational capacity up or down based on dynamic threat levels
- Leverage mature, commercially available or rapidly adaptable systems rather than initiating high-risk developmental programs
The market survey comes as the Air Force races to develop an arsenal of capabilities to defend its installations against drone threat.
“The Government envisions an initial prototype deployment at two designated Continental United States Air Force installations, with option mechanisms to scale across additional ACC installations upon proven performance,” the document states.
Interested firms have until Oct. 31 to respond to the solicitation. ACC is interested in companies that can provide technology for detecting, tracking, and identifying drones—ranging from small quadcopters to larger, Group 3 systems like the Iranian Shahed one-way attack drones that weight up to 1,320 pounds—at distances of up to five miles from a base perimeter, the document states.
Firms should also be capable of incorporating “government-approved kinetic and/or nonkinetic” effectors that range from radio frequency jamming to directed-energy such as lasers and high-powered microwave systems, the document states. Interested defense firms would also have to show they would continuously refresh software and hardware “within a multiyear service contract without frequent contract modifications,” according to the document.
ACC would also want a commercial capability to have the built-in logistical support to be self-sufficient for up to 96 hours, the document states.
The concept would require the contractor to “provide a complete, integrated, turn-key service solution covering materiel, personnel, training, sustainment, and ongoing modernization,” the solicitation states.
It’s unclear how this commercial service would align with the service’s intent to create a new point defense career field for enlisted Airmen, training and equipping them to defend air bases from drone and missile attack. The Air Force is slated to start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. As a short-term fix, the service has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Currently, the Air Force is equipping installations with the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
The service is also acquiring additional counter-drone systems through the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. In the future, counter-drone technology will fall under the “point defense weapon system,” a classification to manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and non-kinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.

articles.title: Britain funds Chornobyl repairs after Russian drone hit
articles.body:
Britain is putting £17 million towards repairing the protective shelter over the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, which was punctured by a Russian drone strike last year, according to the government.
The money forms part of an international programme coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development alongside the Ukrainian government and G7 donors, and will pay for work to restore the structure’s confinement and ventilation functions and protect its intended lifespan. Corrosion threatens to undermine decades of international investment and create longer term environmental and safety risks if the damage is left.
John Healey, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, said: “As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable. We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks.”
Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, said: “Our message to Putin is clear, we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail. Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine’s security, raising the cost of Russia’s aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace.”
The structure in question is the New Safe Confinement, the arch built over the remains of reactor four and the Soviet-era sarcophagus around it, which was slid into position in 2016 and handed over in 2019 after an international effort costing around €1.5 billion. It was designed to hold for a century while the reactor underneath is dismantled, and its outer skin and ventilation system are what keep moisture out of the space where that work has to happen. A drone strike that breaches it turns a sealed structure into one that corrodes.
Attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have continued through the autumn at a heavy rate. Between 5 and 11 October Russia carried out more than two hundred strikes on electricity infrastructure and a further seventeen on oil and gas facilities, six of them after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. On 13 October Russia fired thirty-nine ballistic missiles at Ukraine in one of the largest such attacks of the war, much of it aimed at energy targets, leaving six hundred thousand civilians without power.
Britain has been involved in nuclear safety at the site for years. It was a founding donor to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account in 2020, when that account took over responsibility for safety in the exclusion zone, and has given €8 million to it, making it the third largest individual donor behind Norway and France.
The Foreign Secretary visited Kyiv last week for the first time since taking office and announced £54 million of winter support, including £20 million in energy funding. The Prime Minister hosted President Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, where he set out a further package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles built by Thales in Belfast.

articles.title: US: Somerville weighs Israel boycott over Gaza genocide
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US: Somerville weighs Israel boycott over Gaza genocide
Lawmakers in Somerville, Massachusetts, are considering an ordinance that would bar the US city from awarding contracts to companies accused of complicity in Israel’s violations of international law, amid growing pressure to sever financial ties with firms linked to Israel's genocide in Gaza.
The proposal follows a November 2025 ballot measure backed by 55.7% of voters, calling for the city to end existing business with, and prohibit future contracts and investments in, companies linked to Israel’s “apartheid, genocide, and illegal occupation of Palestine”.
The City Council has delayed a decision to assess the ordinance’s scope and financial impact, with a vote expected on 27 October, according to local reports.
Following renewed discussions on Tuesday led by Somerville’s Legislative Matters Committee, councillors said more time was needed to assess which businesses would be affected and the potential financial implications for the city.
Two Jewish councillors have raised concerns about the proposal, particularly over which companies would fall within its scope.
If enacted, Somerville would join a growing number of US cities adopting divestment measures in line with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, which seeks to hold Israel accountable for its violations of Palestinian rights through economic pressure.
However, the passage of last year's ballot measure prompted a backlash from pro-Israel groups, which have been pressuring the city to reject the proposed ordinance, citing Somerville’s longstanding Jewish community, which is made up of around 84,000 residents.
Jewish opposition to Israel's policies has grown in the US, with many challenging attempts to portray criticism of Israel or support for Palestinian rights as inherently antisemitic.
An October 2025 survey, reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, found that 39% of American Jews believed Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
More recently, a July 2026 Associated Press-NORC poll highlighted deep divisions within Jewish communities over Israel's military actions. Around four in ten religiously unaffiliated Jewish respondents believed Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, compared with around a quarter of religiously affiliated Jewish respondents.
A separate September 2026 survey by the Jewish Electorate Institute found that 61% of American Jewish voters held an unfavourable view of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while 60% wanted him replaced.
The findings underline the diversity of Jewish opinion on Israel, even as pro-Israel groups continue to challenge divestment campaigns.
Somerville for Palestine (S4P), a local organisation that spearheaded both the ballot initiative and the proposed ordinance, has continued to press the council to implement the measure.
The group supports the BDS movement, which has long called for boycotts and divestment from companies it considers complicit in Israeli apartheid and genocide in Gaza.
Pro-Palestine activists have accused the city of maintaining financial ties with companies targeted by the BDS movement.
They point to city records showing that its pension fund has more than $500,000 invested in Lockheed Martin, a weapons manufacturer whose fighter jets and Hellfire missiles have reportedly played a significant role in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Activists have also highlighted more than $1.7 million in contracts Somerville has awarded to Hewlett-Packard over several decades.
According to the BDS movement, HP-linked technology has been used in biometric surveillance systems at Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank, which Palestinians and rights groups have condemned as part of Israel’s system of apartheid.
The ballot initiative and proposed ordinance have received backing from several Somerville councillors, including Ben Ewen-Campen, Ben Wheeler, Wilfred N. Mbah and Jon Link. Jewish Voice for Peace Boston has also voiced support for the measures, demonstrating that Jewish organisations are among those backing efforts to hold Israel accountable through divestment.
The campaign comes amid growing calls for local councils across the US, North America and the wider Western world to recognise the Gaza genocide and sever financial ties with companies accused of facilitating violations of international law.
Pro-Palestine campaigners are urging councils to divest from arms manufacturers supplying Israel with weapons and military technology, as well as companies involved in financing or constructing illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
Somerville’s debate follows a decision by Montreal’s city council in Canada to pass an amended motion in August expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people and civilians affected by hostilities across the Middle East.
The move followed a backlash from pro-Israel groups against an earlier proposal calling on the city to recognise and condemn “apartheid” and “genocide” in Palestine and immediately suspend institutional ties with the Israeli government, its institutions and municipalities.

articles.title: Ukraine to resume refinery strikes amid dispute with US
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country would resume hitting Russian oil refineries and adopted a noticeably more defiant tone towards U.S. President Donald Trump in an interview published on Oct. 15 by the Financial Times.
Since Trump returned to power, Washington’s support for Ukraine has fluctuated alongside his unexpected social media remarks, which have often taken Moscow and Kiev by surprise.
Trump last week unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was never publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
But after a wave of renewed Russian strikes on facilities on Oct. 14, Zelensky told the FT: “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done.”
Russia said on Oct. 15 that Ukraine had attacked an oil refinery in Ryazan, south of the capital, Moscow.
Since Russia launched its invasion in 2022, Ukraine has faced repeated strikes on its power infrastructure and gradually expanded what it says are retaliatory strikes into Russian territory, including on refineries.
Trump criticized the attacks, especially after he struck a surprise diesel deal with Moscow and ordered Ukraine to stop targeting Russian refineries.
Zelensky said Ukraine paused the strikes for several days, despite Russian claims, denied by Kiev, that Ukraine attempted to target refineries during that period.
Despite complying, Zelensky said Ukraine saw its access to key U.S. military capabilities and intelligence restricted.
Starshield, the satellite network built on Starlink and used by militaries, was slowed over on Oct. 14.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” Zelensky told the FT.
He also warned of a “dangerous” cutting off of intelligence sharing with Kiev, which relies heavily on early warnings to protect its cities from Russian air attacks.
Fears that Washington could curb intelligence cooperation had already surfaced after a public clash between Trump and Zelensky early in Trump’s presidency.
The Ukrainian presidency has since worked to smooth relations with Washington, trying to adapt to Trump’s fluctuating stances.
In the interview, Zelensky made a pointed comment about the relationship between Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump “speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong”, he said.
Zelensky also urged the United States not to stand with the aggressor on Oct. 15, calling for “honesty.”
“We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” Zelensky said on social media.

articles.title: Taiwan seeks 462 extended-range air defense missiles for NASAMS
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is seeking 462 extended-range missiles for 12 US-made National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS) to strengthen its air defenses and protect critical infrastructure.
The first phase of the procurement includes 123 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile Extended Range (AMRAAM-ER) missiles. The US has yet to announce the exact number for the second phase, but Taiwan hopes to acquire 462 across both phases, per Liberty Times.
The AMRAAM-ER has an effective interception range of up to 50 kilometers and a maximum altitude of about 25 kilometers. Its range is roughly 50% greater than that of the AIM-120C-7 missiles previously used by NASAMS, more than three times that of Taiwan’s land-based Sky Sword II missiles, and more than 10 times that of the Stinger missiles used by Taiwan’s Avenger air defense systems.
A military official told Liberty Times on Thursday that the US Air Force awarded Raytheon a contract in April to prepare for large-scale AMRAAM-ER production. The contract covers foreign military sales to countries including Taiwan, Hungary, and the Netherlands.
Taiwan’s Air Force plans to deploy NASAMS as a distributed network, with centralized command and control and launchers positioned at multiple locations. Each of the 12 systems would have three launch vehicles carrying six missiles apiece, for a combined capacity of 216 ready-to-fire missiles.
If Taiwan acquires all 462 planned missiles and fully loads the launchers, 246 would remain in reserve, Liberty Times reported. Those missiles would be stored in protected facilities for reloading after an initial engagement.
NASAMS has also been deployed in Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks. By February 2025, the systems had made about 900 successful interceptions there, with a reported success rate of 94%, according to Norwegian military figures cited by Euromaidan Press. Nearly 60% of the intercepted targets were cruise missiles.

articles.title: Iran's deputy FM visits Lebanon amid diplomatic tensions
articles.body:

Iran's deputy FM visits Lebanon amid diplomatic tensions
Iran's deputy foreign minister Saeed Khatibzadeh held talks with Lebanese officials in Beirut on Thursday in an apparent effort to ease mounting diplomatic tensions between the two countries, following Lebanon's refusal to recognise Tehran's newly appointed ambassador.
The visit coincided with a phone call between Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, signalling a possible attempt to repair relations after months of strained relations over Iran's influence in Lebanon and its support for Hezbollah.
Lebanon has expressed willingness to turn the page with Tehran, provided ties are based on mutual respect, sovereignty and non-interference in each other's internal affairs.
However, Lebanese officials remain concerned that Hezbollah could once again draw the country into a wider regional conflict in support of Iran, particularly amid fears of renewed military escalation involving Tehran, Washington and Israel.
Khatibzadeh met Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri at his Ain el-Tineh residence in Beirut on Thursday, with Iran's chargé d'affaires in Lebanon, Tawfiq Samadi, also attending.
The discussions focused on developments in Lebanon and the wider region, including Israel's continued attacks on Lebanese territory and its refusal to withdraw from the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Following the meeting, Khatibzadeh emphasised the longstanding relationship between the two countries.
"I conveyed my warmest wishes to the Lebanese people and to Lebanon, this great country with which we share longstanding and friendly relations at various levels," he said.
He added that such visits were a natural part of bilateral relations, serving not only to exchange views but also to strengthen coordination between Beirut and Tehran.
The Iranian official arrived in Beirut on Wednesday, where he was received by representatives of Hezbollah and the Amal Movement.
He also met Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, deputy head of Lebanon's Higher Islamic Shia Council, to discuss regional developments and the prospects for the coming period.
During the meeting, Khatibzadeh outlined Iran's position on ongoing contacts and negotiations with the United States.
Lebanon insists on sovereignty and diplomacy
The diplomatic outreach follows Wednesday's telephone conversation between Aoun and Araghchi, during which the two officials discussed recent regional developments and agreed on the importance of pursuing diplomatic solutions to end conflicts across the Middle East.
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab's Arabic-language sister publication, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, that Beirut remained open to relations with Iran based on mutual respect and non-interference.
The sources said Lebanon had previously asked Tehran to nominate a new ambassador to Beirut but remained firm in its rejection of attempts to turn the country into an arena for regional conflicts.
"Lebanon is tired of wars and refuses to continue being dragged into them," the sources said, adding that the country was still paying the price of previous conflicts involving Hezbollah.
They also expressed concern over escalating rhetoric from Hezbollah and continuing Israeli threats, while stressing that Beirut remained committed to negotiations despite the difficulties involved.
"There is no solution except diplomacy, not war," the sources said.
The visit has nevertheless drawn criticism from Lebanese political figures opposed to Hezbollah.
Kataeb Party leader and MP Samy Gemayel rejected Khatibzadeh's presence in Beirut, posting the words "persona non grata" in Persian on X on Wednesday.
Ambassador dispute deepens tensions
Relations between Beirut and Tehran have deteriorated in recent months, particularly over Iran's opposition to Lebanese government decisions aimed at placing all weapons under state control.
Lebanese authorities have accused Tehran of interfering in the country's internal affairs through its political and military support for Hezbollah.
Tensions intensified following the regional escalation in March, when Lebanon adopted a tougher stance towards Tehran following Iranian attacks on Arab and Gulf states.
The Lebanese government also introduced stricter measures concerning Iranian nationals after Israeli airstrikes targeted two hotels in and around Beirut during the March 2026 offensive.
Israel claimed that members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were staying at the hotels and threatened further attacks against Iranian personnel in Lebanon.
The diplomatic dispute escalated after Tehran appointed Mohammad Reza Raouf Sheibani as its new ambassador to Beirut, replacing Mojtaba Amani, who was injured in Israel's pager attacks on 17 September 2024.
On 24 March, Lebanese authorities withdrew recognition of Sheibani's diplomatic accreditation and ordered him to leave the country.
He remained in Lebanon despite the decision and was subsequently granted a courtesy residency permit.
Khatibzadeh's visit also comes amid renewed attention to Iranian financial support for Hezbollah.
On Tuesday, Hezbollah announced financial assistance for displaced Lebanese families and those whose homes had been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable by Israeli attacks.
The announcement coincided with reports that Hezbollah had received $200 million in funding from Iran, although the US State Department issued statements disputing the existence of the alleged funds.

articles.title: Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, notably Al-Jazeera offices in Doha, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru—a spyware company blacklisted by the US government—as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separatereports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads—often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods—reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements—called cookie matching—allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine—any site—you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

articles.body:
The U.S. military has developed new plans for possible strikes on Iran that include using the so-called "mother of all bombs" against infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders attacks to resume, either before or after the U.S. midterm elections, CNN reported, citing American officials familiar with the matter.
Deploying the GBU-43/B, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a significant escalation.
However, sources familiar with internal U.S. military discussions told CNN that doubts remain over whether the weapon could achieve Trump's stated strategic objectives or significantly alter the course of the war.
One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iran, including "numerous energy infrastructure targets" and the possible use of the MOAB. The source said the wording used was that the strikes would take place "before the U.S. withdrawal from the area of responsibility of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM)," suggesting the administration could launch further attacks, seek to declare victory and rapidly withdraw all its forces.
Another source told CNN that military plans to strike Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly call for the use of the MOAB. Trump has repeatedly threatened in recent months to attack Pickaxe Mountain, where the United States and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program.
However, questions remain about the MOAB's effectiveness against Iran's nuclear facilities and other sites buried deep underground. The GPS-guided bomb can destroy an area equivalent to nine city blocks, but some officials believe it is unlikely to penetrate deeply enough to destroy suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe Mountain, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite, or other Iranian nuclear sites that remain intact.
The "mother of all bombs" has been used in combat only once, in Afghanistan in 2017. It was developed in the run-up to the Iraq War and first tested in 2003. Following its deployment against tunnels used by ISIS terrorists in Afghanistan nearly a decade ago, a U.S. military spokesman said the bomb contained approximately 11 tons of explosives. Because of its enormous size, it was dropped from the rear of a U.S. Air Force C-130 transport aircraft.
Production of GBU bombs began in the 1990s, with the weapons designed to strike surface targets rather than underground bunkers. They became increasingly common with the introduction of GPS guidance technology, which significantly improved their accuracy. Development of the GBU-43 began in 2002, and the bomb could only be carried by a C-130 Hercules aircraft. Once released from the plane, it is guided to its target by GPS.

articles.title: Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch
articles.body:
The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years.
In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch, consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems.
This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops.
The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields.
Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch.
“When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there.
After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground.
Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation.
“Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.”
Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years.
The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems.
He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details.
As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude.
“That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.”
Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems.
As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network. Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted.
He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year.
“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said.

A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.

"The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran's attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage," he said.
The White House and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on 28 February, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea - the world's most widely used fertiliser - and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertiliser shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertiliser products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
Five vessels a day
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," said Moreira da Silva, who is also the executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertiliser supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
Multiple shipping chokepoints
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz."
(Reuters)

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia unleashes 850 Shahed drones as Ukraine faces restrictions on its defenses
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia unleashes 850 Shahed drones as Ukraine faces restrictions on its defenses
The Ukrainian President wrote this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
“Emergency services are still providing assistance in dozens of our cities and communities. Repair crews and rescuers are working to deal with the aftermath of Russian attacks. For practically all of yesterday and throughout last night, a massive Shahed attack was underway. The drones kept coming in waves, and there was not a single hour when our skies were clear of them. From midnight yesterday through 9:00 today, there had already been more than 850 Shaheds – and this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted. We managed to shoot down some of the Shaheds. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelensky stressed.
He noted that Kirovohrad region had suffered one of the largest attacks. Strikes were also reported in Kyiv and the surrounding region, the Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Rivne, Kharkiv and Donetsk regions, as well as the Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Poltava and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Three people were killed in Kropyvnytskyi and another three in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such opportunity and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the previous day, Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, a technology adviser to the President of Ukraine, said that SpaceX had introduced restrictions overnight on the operating speed of Starlink terminals while in motion, without giving Ukraine’s Defense Forces advance notice.
The Ministry of Defense reported that, as of Wednesday evening, SpaceX was maintaining a speed limit of 161 km/h for Starshield terminals (the “military package”) while in motion. During the day, the actual restrictions were considerably stricter.
The Ministry of Defense stressed that the Starlink restrictions detected overnight had complicated the operation of the Defense Forces’ unmanned systems, logistics and middle-strike capabilities.

articles.title: Startup’s laser turns Rheinmetall autonomous cargo vehicle into drone killer
articles.body:
- Aurelius Systems is displaying its Archimedes autonomous counter-drone laser on an American Rheinmetall unmanned ground vehicle at AUSA 2026.
- The startup raised $40 million in August and says Archimedes can defeat small and medium drones at more than a kilometer.
Aurelius Systems is showing its Archimedes autonomous laser weapon mounted on an American Rheinmetall unmanned ground vehicle at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington this week, where the two companies are pitching mobile laser defense against small drones to U.S. Army buyers.
The San Francisco-based startup said in a post on X that Archimedes is on display in motion at the Rheinmetall booth through the end of the show, as part of the companies’ partnership to bring counter-drone lasers to uncrewed combat vehicles.
Archimedes is a lightweight turret that combines a high-power laser with machine vision and radar, and Aurelius says it can find, track and burn down a drone on its own without an operator initiating each engagement. The system is aimed at Group 1 and Group 2 drones, the small and medium-size types that include commercial quadcopters and many of the one-way attack drones used in Ukraine, and the company says it can defeat them at more than a kilometer.
The two firms announced their partnership in July. According to Tectonic, Archimedes is being integrated first on the Ox, the unmanned ground vehicle American Rheinmetall has entered in the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport competition for a vehicle that hauls supplies and equipment over rough terrain. With a laser on board, a cargo-carrying vehicle can defend itself against drones during resupply runs, a role Rheinmetall has described as protection for autonomous logistics missions.
Aurelius first showed the laser on a Rheinmetall vehicle at the Reindustrialize 2026 conference in Detroit in June, in a display built with American Rheinmetall and electric vehicle startup Harbinger.
In August, the company raised a $40 million Series A round co-led by Draper Associates and KAS Venture Partners to scale up Archimedes production. During the Pentagon’s T-REX 26-2 experimentation event, the laser downed more than 20 quadcopters and more than five drones supplied by the U.S. Army, Tectonic reported, and at the U.S. Army’s Operation Jailbreak exercise at Fort Carson, Colorado, Aurelius linked Archimedes with Anduril’s Lattice software and the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense command and control system, which ties sensors and shooters together.
Lasers appeal to militaries because each shot costs only the electricity needed to fire it, compared with tens of thousands of dollars or more for a missile interceptor, and Aurelius says it builds Archimedes largely from commercially available parts to keep the system’s own price down.

articles.title: Kuwait drone shield to cover the sea as well as the air
articles.body:
The counter-drone system Kuwait is buying from the British firm MARSS will defend against seaborne drones along the coast as well as airborne ones, using sonar alongside radar and electro-optical sensors feeding a network of command centres, according to the company.
MARSS, an EOS company, will act as prime contractor and systems integrator on the £370 million contract, installing sensors across a network of sites that report into central command centres. Its NiDAR command and control platform fuses that data into threat assessments and provides what the company describes as hemispherical coverage against airborne and coastal seaborne drones. The contract also covers an initial supply of hard-kill interceptors and soft-kill jammers.
Johannes Pinl, chief executive of MARSS, said: “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system. It is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that.
“Over the coming 24 months, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.”
Doctor Andreas Schwer, chief executive of EOS, said: “Air defence is being redefined by the drone. Nations can no longer afford to answer low-cost threats with high-cost interceptors, and they need integrated systems that can respond faster than the threat. MARSS’ NiDAR is the intelligence layer in EOS’ counter-drone strategy, connecting sensors and effectors into a single, scalable architecture. Kuwait’s decision to deploy this capability nationwide shows where the market is heading, and it positions EOS as a leading provider of integrated counter-drone defence.”
Having both soft-kill and hard-kill effectors run through the same command system gives operators layered defeat options and a choice of response for each engagement, the company said, with NiDAR using AI to classify threats automatically and recommend an engagement, shortening the time between detection and defeat.
MARSS said the contract builds on NiDAR systems it has already fielded in the Gulf, which it said have been in operational use throughout the recent crisis in the region, and extends that approach to a national scale.
Delivery will be phased over 24 months and followed by a multi-year integrated logistic support programme. A training package running over several months will put MARSS personnel on the ground to train Kuwaiti operators across the sensors, the effectors and NiDAR itself, and a team will deploy to Kuwait for the duration, with recruitment already under way.
The commercial side of the deal was announced by the Ministry of Defence earlier, including the £370 million value, the roughly one hundred jobs expected across MARSS and its British supply chain, production proposed for Bristol, and the contract’s place within Taskforce Sabre, the government and industry effort to help Gulf states buy what they need quickly. Britain has already supplied Kuwait with the Rapid Sentry ground-based air defence missile system, and the Royal Air Force’s ORCUS counter-drone system is operating in the country.
NiDAR itself covers air, surface, sub-surface and land, detecting, tracking and classifying threats and recommending responses, and MARSS says it has more than sixty deployments worldwide. The company has been working on AI-enabled command and control for around twenty years, including research with the European Union, NATO and defence agencies.
EOS is an Australian group listed on the ASX with divisions covering defence and space. Its defence products include remote weapon stations, high energy laser weapons and drone interceptors, and NiDAR sits inside that portfolio as the command layer. MARSS is exhibiting NiDAR at SOFEX in Jordan from 27 to 29 October, where it will be shown integrated onto vehicle platforms alongside EOS remote weapon stations.

FSB Recruited Kyiv Teen on Telegram to Register 148 Starlinks for Russian Troops, SBU Says
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detained an alleged Federal Security Service (FSB) agent in Kyiv who attempted to activate 148 Starlink terminals for Russia, the SBU reported on October 14.
According to the SBU, the operation prevented one of the largest known batches of Starlink satellite terminals from being registered for Russian use. The agency stated that Russian forces intended to use the terminals to plan combat operations in the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Starlink has become central to Ukrainian combat operations, providing satellite connectivity for command links, real-time drone video, artillery coordination, and unmanned strike missions. Ukrainian forces have also used Starlink-connected drones for medium-range attacks on Russian logistics, while Kyiv has sought expanded access to support deeper strikes against military targets.
Investigators identified the suspect as an 18-year-old former student at a Kyiv college who had trained as a welder. The SBU stated that he was recruited after searching Telegram channels for quick ways to earn money.
According to the investigation, an FSB officer contacted the teenager through one of the chats and offered him payment in exchange for cooperation.
The SBU reported that within several days of his recruitment, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances.
Investigators stated that he then prepared false personal data to register another 133 terminals for the Russian security service.
Counterintelligence officers detained the suspect near a post office as he allegedly prepared to activate another batch of Starlink terminals. The SBU also blocked terminals that had already been registered after the suspect transmitted their credentials to his Russian handler through a messaging app.
Several smartphones containing what investigators described as evidence of his cooperation with Russia were seized during searches.
The suspect was notified of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 111 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, covering high treason committed under martial law.
He remains in custody without the right to bail and faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property if convicted.
Earlier on October 14, Ukrainian forces reported disruptions to Starlink-based battlefield communications that forced some drone units to cancel missions. The restrictions affected Starshield connections used to control unmanned aircraft, with Ukrainian troops reporting signal losses during flight.

"The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times, arguing that Ukraine had paused energy strikes for three days to comply with the U.S.-announced "energy ceasefire," while Moscow continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Trump scraps plan to livestream execution after broad backlash
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump scraps plan to livestream execution after global condemnation
The firing squad execution of a convicted military base shooter will not be livestreamed, US President Donald Trump announced Thursday, canceling a contentious plan by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The move to livestream Nidal Hasan's execution was widely opposed at home and abroad, prompting outrage from both US Democratic and Republican politicians, the Catholic Church and the United Nations.
The cancellation is a blow to Hegseth, who is already under fire over the stalemated Iran war and its fallout, which are weighing on Trump's Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections.
Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.
The US president indicated he did not personally oppose the streaming plan, saying it "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die," Trump said, adding that the execution could still be viewed in person by immediate family of the victims if they wanted to do so.
Hasan's execution - scheduled for 3 December at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 - is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945.
Hegseth said last week that "we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," later confirming that the plan was to livestream the execution.
"People need to understand that...there's serious consequence for these types of things," he said.
Most Americans opposed
Backlash to the plan quickly grew following Hegseth's announcement.
The United Nations said streaming the execution would amount to "torture," while the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops said it was a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death," and both Australia and Britain's prime ministers described it as "abhorrent."
Vice President JD Vance, who recently released a memoir on his Catholic faith, said he would not watch the execution if the plan went forward.
A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Thursday found that eight in 10 Americans opposed the livestreaming of the execution.
Lawmakers from both main US parties have said they are against it, including top House Republican Mike Johnson, who said it could be a "recruiting tool for future terrorists."
Dozens of retired US military officers also warned in an open letter against broadcasting the execution.
It "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," and "will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers," said the officers, including more than 40 generals and admirals.
The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.
The Death Penalty Information Center says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916.
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 - six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.
He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.
The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military's occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
(AFP)

articles.title: Trump and Netanyahu unlikely to strike Iran before elections, but Israel fears surprise attack
articles.body:
Israel's political and security establishment widely believes that neither Israel nor the United States will launch an attack on Iran before their respective elections, with just 12 days remaining until Israelis vote and less than three weeks until the U.S. midterms. However, Israeli officials remain concerned that an Iranian provocation, an attack by Tehran's regional proxies or a military miscalculation could trigger a confrontation despite efforts to avoid one.
The prevailing assessment is that President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are unwilling to risk a new military campaign ahead of the elections. Netanyahu is particularly concerned that renewed fighting with Iran could damage Likud's chances of remaining in power in the October 27 vote.
The possibility of an attack was discussed during a conversation between Netanyahu and Trump last week. Although Israeli officials generally consider a preelection strike unlikely, they still regard the possibility as significant.
One concern is that Iran or the Houthi rebels in Yemen could provoke an Israeli response through a limited operation or an attack carried out by one of Tehran's regional proxies.
Another is the possibility of a miscalculation, with each side interpreting the other's military preparations as evidence of an imminent attack and deciding to strike first.
Israel has conveyed a warning to Washington that if Iran makes such a move, it will face an exceptionally severe response, potentially unprecedented in scale, even after the thousands of Iranian targets struck by Israel and the United States during the war.
Israeli security forces are therefore maintaining a high state of alert and preparing for possible surprise attacks by Iran, Hezbollah or the Houthis.
Security officials have emphasized that any Israeli decision to attack Iran ultimately depends on Trump. Without the American president's approval, they say, Israel would be unable to carry out such an operation.
Trump does not appear to have reached a final decision and is continuing to weigh his options. Officials familiar with the matter said he blocked at least two planned Israeli strikes during the summer, both based on Israeli intelligence indicating that Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear program.
Earlier Thursday, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir conducted a situation assessment and operational briefing at Central Command, warning commanders that the danger of escalation had increased.
"Given the numerous warnings across all fronts and the sensitivity of the current period, the potential for escalation has increased," Zamir said.
The military chief also recently warned senior American government and military officials that renewed hostilities with Iran could lead to the postponement of Israel's parliamentary election.
Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, issued a similar warning Thursday ahead of a Security Council meeting, saying he had delivered a direct message to Iran and Hezbollah.
"Do not try to exploit Israel's election period. Anyone who dares attack us will suffer a devastating blow," Danon said.
An Israeli security official assessed Wednesday that another military campaign resembling previous operations would be unlikely to produce a fundamentally different outcome without an American ground operation.
"There is an understanding that without a ground operation by the Americans, there is no chance of achieving something different and new," the official said, adding that repeating previous military actions before the U.S. elections would be a political disaster for Trump.
The president has sent conflicting signals in recent days. During a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday, he threatened another major strike against Iran.
"Just wait and see what we do to Iran. We're going to hit them hard. Just wait and see what we do to Iran, because we're getting pretty fed up," Trump said.
Yet last week, Trump declared that he would not attack Iran again before the November 3 midterm elections.
For Israeli officials, the uncertainty means that while a deliberate strike before the elections remains unlikely, the risk of an unexpected escalation has not disappeared. The greatest concern is that an Iranian move, or an attack by one of its proxies, could force decisions neither Washington nor Jerusalem currently wants to make.

articles.title: Britain to fit its own kit to Ukraine donated weapons
articles.body:
Britain will retrofit British capability onto equipment given to Ukraine by other partners, the Prime Minister told President Zelensky at Downing Street, alongside a fresh package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles and talks on accelerating long range support before winter, according to the government.
Andy Burnham welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday afternoon, and the two began by reflecting on their call the previous Saturday and on what the government described as Russia’s blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure since President Trump called for an energy ceasefire. It was clear Russia had no interest in peace, the leaders underlined.
On how Ukraine’s allies could step up, particularly against Russia’s barrage of jet-powered drones, the Prime Minister set out the latest British package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles. He added that Britain would continue to develop innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners.
On long range missiles, the leaders discussed how Britain could accelerate defensive support ahead of the winter, and the Prime Minister said Britain would continue diplomatic efforts to support international supplies of defensive equipment.
Donated equipment arrives in Ukraine from more than fifty countries in a bewildering variety of types and standards, much of it Soviet-era, some of it decades old, and a great deal of it without the sensors, communications or guidance that would let it work inside a modern targeting chain. Fitting British seekers, fuzes, datalinks or electronic warfare packages onto someone else’s donated hardware turns a stock problem into an integration problem, and the British defence industry is better placed to solve the second than the first.
Britain has already done something along those lines at a smaller scale. Stone Cloak, the tablet-sized jammer designed by the government to stop Russian air defences tracking the drones it is fitted to, is manufactured under a British contract and its intellectual property has been handed to Ukraine so that Ukrainian industry can mass-produce it.
Jet-powered drones are the specific threat behind the latest missile package. The Geran-3, a jet version of the Shahed-136 design, flies considerably faster than the propeller-driven type Ukraine has been shooting down since 2022, which compresses the time available to detect, track and engage and pushes targets out of reach of the machine guns and small arms that handle the slower ones. Lightweight Multirole Missiles are one of the few interceptors cheap enough to use against them in quantity.
Thales builds those missiles in Belfast, where production now runs at four times its 2022 rate with £100 million committed to expanding further. The company says the work sustains 1,100 direct jobs in Northern Ireland and around 700 more across its British supply chain.

articles.title: Ukrainian cruise missiles hit six Su-34 bombers deep inside Russia

Satellite imagery of Russia’s Borisoglebsk air base shows that a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike destroyed four Su-34 fighter-bombers and badly damaged two more, backing up the Ukrainian Navy’s claim that it hit six of the jets on the night of Oct. 14–15.
The images, published by the Ukrainian aviation monitoring channel AviVector, compare the airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region before and after the attack. Pictures taken on Oct. 13 show six Su-34s parked at the spot that was later struck, while the post-strike imagery shows four of them completely destroyed and two with significant damage. Numerous pro-Russian Telegram channels have also acknowledged the losses.
The Ukrainian Navy said it attacked Borisoglebsk with its Neptune coastal missile system and that the strike hit six Su-34M bombers, the modernized version of the aircraft, and destroyed equipment used to support flight operations. Secondary explosions and a fire followed at the base, the Navy said.
“The destruction of enemy Su-34Ms significantly weakens the enemy’s aviation potential and reduces the intensity of tactical aviation use in the relevant areas of the front,” the Ukrainian Navy said.
The Su-34 is the main aircraft Russia uses to drop heavy guided glide bombs on Ukrainian troop positions and frontline towns. Fitted with wing kits, those bombs can be released tens of kilometers from the target, outside the reach of many Ukrainian short-range air defenses, which makes the bombers themselves a priority target for Kyiv.
Borisoglebsk hosts the 783rd training aviation center, one of the main schools for Russian strike and bomber pilots, along with units of the 105th composite aviation division that fly Su-34, Su-35S and Su-30SM jets, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. Residents reported a missile alert and a series of explosions in the town on the evening of Oct. 14.
The strike came days after Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation delivered a new batch of Su-34s to the Russian Aerospace Forces.
Ukraine developed the Neptune as an anti-ship missile, and it became widely known after two of them sank the Russian Black Sea Fleet flagship Moskva in April 2022. Ukrainian engineers have since adapted the missile for strikes on land targets, and longer-range versions have hit military sites deep inside Russia.
The Ukrainian Navy said it is still assessing the full results of the attack on Borisoglebsk, including damage to support equipment and infrastructure at the base.

articles.title: UAVs with AI control will bypass air defense systems – Ukraine is preparing a large-scale operation to block airports in russia

UAVs with AI control will bypass air defense systems – Ukraine is preparing a large-scale operation to block airports in russia
Kyiv • UNN
Operation M&Ms has already caused thousands of flight delays and cancellations in Moscow. The next stage could involve AI-powered drones.
Ukraine plans to significantly intensify an operation to disrupt the work of Russian airports, which has already caused large-scale flight delays and cancellations in Moscow. The next stage may involve the use of artificial intelligence-powered drones capable of bypassing air defenses. The Atlantic reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to Ukrainian officials involved in developing the operation, so far the drones have mainly forced the Russian authorities to close the airspace near airports without directly striking aviation infrastructure.
However, even this tactic has already created serious problems. From October 3 to 9, 345 flights were canceled at Moscow airports, while nearly 4,000 were delayed. On October 10 alone, 692 flights were delayed and 93 had to be canceled.
Ukraine is preparing artificial intelligence-powered drones for a new stage of the operation
According to The Atlantic, the operation has been named M&Ms. Its next stage involves the use of artificial intelligence-powered drones that will be able to independently bypass Russian air defenses and attack airports directly.
The publication's sources claim that such drones will not require American intelligence data, and that their mass production is planned to be established in the near future.
One such aircraft has allegedly already been used during hostilities in Donbas. At the same time, development of the technology is still ongoing, and these drones have not yet been used against Russian airports.
The scale of the problems facing Russian aviation is also demonstrated by the situation on October 9, when two Moscow airports were out of operation for seven hours because of a drone attack. According to the publication, even Vladimir Putin's plane was unable to land in Moscow after returning from Turkmenistan.

articles.title: iPhones floating in Strait of Hormuz: viral footage emerges after Iranian attack sinks cargo ship
articles.body:
Media outlets across the Arab world circulated footage Thursday evening purportedly showing iPhones floating in the Strait of Hormuz following one of Iran's latest attacks on ships in the strategic trade route.
The footage shows shipping containers floating at sea, surrounded by numerous small objects. People aboard small boats, whose identities remain unclear, can be seen collecting the valuable goods scattered in the water. One of the boats appears to be loaded with boxes of iPhones. One report claimed the devices were Apple's latest model, the iPhone 18.
Although the origin of the containers scattered across the Strait of Hormuz remains unclear, the footage emerged a day after Iran announced that a vessel carrying 2,500 containers had sunk in the strait after allegedly entering a "dangerous route" without Iranian authorization and striking a mine.
Iranian reports did not identify the ship, but Reuters reported Wednesday, citing maritime industry sources, that the GFS Pride, a small Singapore-flagged container ship with a capacity of 2,824 containers, had sunk after being struck by a projectile. That would indicate the vessel was directly attacked rather than hitting a previously laid mine.
Singapore confirmed that the ship sank after a fire broke out aboard it, adding that all 21 crew members had been safely evacuated without injuries.
The Associated Press reported that two Singaporean cargo ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz were attacked Tuesday and Wednesday, with the second vessel continuing to its destination.
According to Reuters, the GFS Pride was the second ship to sink in the strait within just 24 hours. A third vessel, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao, also sank after sustaining severe damage in an earlier attack on Sept. 23.
Although Iran has attacked numerous vessels throughout the war in an effort to block the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for the global oil trade, ships sinking as a result of these attacks remains extremely rare. Including the two latest vessels, only three ships have sunk since the war began in late February.
The iPhones and other goods seen drifting in the waters of Hormuz most likely came from the GFS Pride, which sank Wednesday. According to a Saudi report Thursday evening, luxury perfumes and other products were also floating in the water.
In recent days, Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have intensified again, in what appears to be an attempt by Tehran to trigger a renewed escalation with the United States just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
President Donald Trump has said he will not attack Iran before the elections, scheduled for Nov. 3.
Reuters reported Wednesday that an analysis of maritime security data and reports submitted to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) showed that the pace of attacks in recent days had reached its highest level since the war began.
A similar rate of attacks was recorded between Oct. 3 and Oct. 5, but another escalation now appears to be underway.
"There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," a maritime security official told Reuters.
The report quoted two senior Iranian officials who said Tehran had adopted a new strategy of stepping up attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and other parts of the Persian Gulf to keep global oil prices high and influence the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections.
According to the officials, the decision to change strategy was made at the highest levels of Iran's leadership and coordinated among the country's various centers of power.
One official said Iran began employing different methods of attacking vessels about 10 days ago, targeting ships it claims are violating restrictions Tehran has imposed on maritime traffic through the strait.
The objective of the escalation, he said, is "to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices."
The second official made clear that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring prices down before the November elections.
"Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it," he said, adding: "This is a game of chess."
The renewed attacks come as the Trump administration claims that despite Iranian threats, maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is gradually returning to normal and oil flows have recovered to levels similar to those recorded before the war, when approximately one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the waterway.
The administration attributes the recovery to a U.S. Navy-led operation to protect shipping in the strait, alongside a continuing blockade of Iranian ports.
Meanwhile, the escalation between Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia is also continuing. Riyadh reported Thursday evening that it had intercepted additional drone attacks launched toward the kingdom by the Yemeni rebels.
The interceptions came hours after Saudi Arabia disclosed that at least 19 people had been killed in Houthi attacks on the kingdom since the beginning of the month and that the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, had been targeted at least 20 times.
At a news conference presenting the figures, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Rayed Krimly accused Iran of "encouraging" the Houthis to escalate their attacks and seize territory overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month.
The move gave the rebels, and their patrons in Tehran, another powerful bargaining chip against the United States.
"We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," Krimly said.
He accused Iran of continuing to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and its commitments under the Beijing Agreement.
He was referring to the 2023 agreement under which Saudi Arabia and Iran restored diplomatic relations after a seven-year rupture.
Krimly noted that Saudi Arabia continues to maintain direct communication channels with Iran, adding that the foreign ministers of the two countries had spoken by telephone even during one of the waves of attacks on Riyadh's airport.
Alongside the renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Houthis also launched an unusual missile attack Thursday evening against the Maashiq presidential palace in Aden, southern Yemen.
The palace houses Yemen's internationally recognized government, whose forces are currently engaged in ground battles with the Houthis for control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Footage circulated from Aden showed smoke rising near the palace. Two Yemeni government officials told Reuters that two security guards were killed in the attack.
Yemen's prime minister and Cabinet ministers were at the palace when the attack occurred, but were reportedly unharmed.
According to reports, five missiles were launched at the compound.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that the attack targeted "the military operations headquarters of the Saudi enemy in Aden."

articles.title: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
articles.body:
The US military has developed new strike plans that include the potential use of the “mother of all bombs” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders a resumption of combat operations, CNN reported Wednesday, citing multiple US officials familiar with the plans.
The proposed use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, would mark a significant escalation in the conflict with Iran, although officials have questioned whether the weapon could achieve Washington’s military objectives.
According to CNN, Trump has directed the military to prepare additional strike options against Iranian targets, including energy infrastructure and facilities associated with the country’s nuclear program. The plans could be activated before or after the upcoming US midterm elections if the president decides to resume major combat operations.
One source familiar with the military planning told CNN that the proposed strikes could take place before a US military withdrawal from the US Central Command area of responsibility, potentially allowing the administration to launch further attacks before declaring victory and withdrawing its forces.
A second source said plans for strikes against Iranian nuclear sites, including a suspected underground facility at Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly included the potential deployment of the MOAB.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to target Pickaxe Mountain, where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear program. The president has maintained that preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remains a central objective of the US campaign.
READ: Axios: Netanyahu discussed joint strike on Iran with Trump before Israeli election
A US official told CNN that military planners routinely prepare a range of options for policymakers, from lower-intensity operations to more powerful strikes against heavily fortified targets.
However, the MOAB’s effectiveness against deeply buried nuclear facilities remains uncertain.
The GPS-guided bomb can devastate a large surface area equivalent to approximately nine city blocks, but it is not designed to penetrate deeply underground. Sources cited by CNN said the weapon would likely struggle to destroy facilities protected by thick layers of granite and other fortifications.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a source familiar with the military planning discussions told CNN, describing it as unsuitable for deep penetration.
If deployed, the bomb could cause extensive destruction at the point of impact, while its large blast radius could raise serious concerns about civilian casualties, particularly if strikes targeted energy infrastructure near populated areas or other civilian facilities.
Despite these limitations, US officials have reportedly considered the weapon’s potential psychological impact as part of the administration’s broader military options.
One source told CNN that the president could face pressure to take further action against Iran despite uncertainty over whether additional strikes would force Tehran to accept Washington’s demands.
The source suggested the MOAB could serve as a means of exerting psychological pressure, particularly given the limitations of available munitions against deeply buried targets.
